title: ggml : allow MUL_MAT_ID -1 index to skip the computation
body:
## Overview

Sorry for the big PR, but unfortunately this change cannot be gated by a graph build-time condition, so I need to add it to all backends at once. Important to note: code is 100% AI-generated.

This change allow `mul_mat_id` to read `-1` index as a sentiment for "skip computation". This allow implement an "expert mask" similar to pytorch impl of MoE.

It's useful for these 2 models:
- https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/15512 --> model has "small" and "big" experts, so it will be split into 2 `mul_mat_id` after this PR, one masked small exp and one masked big exp
- https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/19182 --> implemented via a correct by sub-optimal solution, need this PR to work properly

<details>

<summary>Details about masking logic</summary>

The masking impl wll be like this:
```
Example on x = [2, 0, 1, 3] ; mask out all exp >= 2 --> expected [-1, 0, 1, -1]
---------------------------------------
x = [2, 0, 1, 3]

Step 1: y = sub(x, 1)
        y = [1, -1, 0, 2]

Step 2: c = clamp(y, 0, 1)
        c = [1, 0, 0, 1]

Step 3: two_c = sub(c, neg(c))
        neg(c) = [-1, 0, 0, -1]
        two_c  = [2, 0, 0, 2]

Step 4: z = clamp(x, -1, 1)
        z = [1, 0, 1, 1]

Step 5: result = sub(z, two_c)
        result = [1-2, 0-0, 1-0, 1-2]
               = [-1, 0, 1, -1]

Final output: [-1, 0, 1, -1]
```

Generalized formula for masking exp >= N:

```
result = clamp(x, -1, N-1) - N * clamp(x - (N-1), 0, 1)
```

</details>

## Additional info

Most backends are covered, but I only tested on Metal.

Some are real skip (computation is skipped), and some is fake mul mat with 0

| Backend | Path | Skips computation? | How |
|---|---|---|---|
| CPU | `ggml-cpu.c` mul_mat_id | Real skip | slot dropped from `matrix_rows`, dst row memset |
| CPU (repack extra buffer) | `repack.cpp` | Real skip | same grouping loop |
| CPU (spacemit IME) | `spacemit/ime.cpp` | Real skip | same grouping loop |
| CUDA / HIP / MUSA | mmq (quantized, batch) | Real skip | excluded from `mm_ids_helper` compaction, `mm_ids_zero_dst` kernel writes 0 |
| CUDA / HIP / MUSA | mmf (float, batch) | Real skip | same |
| CUDA / HIP / MUSA | mmvf (float, bs=1) | Real skip | block returns before reading src0, writes 0 |
| CUDA / HIP / MUSA | mmvq (quantized, bs=1) | Real skip | block/warp returns before reading src0, writes 0 |
| CUDA / HIP / MUSA | generic cuBLAS fallback | Real skip | slot dropped from the host-side sort, dst row zeroed after the scatter |
| Metal | `kernel_mul_mm_id` (batch >= 32) | Real skip | `map0` marks the slot 0xFFFF so no expert claims it, `kernel_mul_mm_id_zero` writes 0 |
| Metal | `kernel_mul_mv_id` (batch < 32) | Real skip | threadgroup returns before reading src0, writes 0 |
| Vulkan | `mul_mm` / `mul_mmq` / `mul_mm_cm2` (batch) | Real skip | excluded by `count_experts` + `load_row_ids`, `count_experts` also writes 0 to the dst row |
| Vulkan | `mul_mat_vec` (bs=1) | **Compute + discard** | shared `get_offsets` clamps the expert to 0, `reduce_result` overwrites with 0 |
| SYCL | batched sort path | Real skip | slot dropped from the counting sort, `k_zero_dst_rows` kernel writes 0 |
| SYCL | `ne12 == 1` per-slot path | Real skip | `ggml_sycl_mul_mat` not called, `memset` instead |
| SYCL | mmvq MoE GEMV (+ reorder) | Real skip | warp returns before reading src0, writes 0 |
| OpenCL | `gemm` MoE (sorted, batch) | Real skip | slot dropped in `kernel_moe_histogram`/`kernel_moe_scatter`, `kernel_moe_zero_dst` writes 0 |
| OpenCL | `gemv_moe_*` and `mul_mv_id_*` | Real skip | workgroup returns before reading src0, `kernel_moe_zero_dst` writes 0 |
| WebGPU | `mul_mat_id` (batch) | Real skip | slot dropped in `mul_mat_id_gather`, same shader writes 0 to the dst row |
| WebGPU | `mul_mat_id_vec` (bs=1) | Real skip | slot never enters `gathered_count_ids`, workgroup 0 writes 0, extra workgroups return |
| Hexagon | `op_matmul_id` (HMX + HVX) | Real skip | `scan_expert_ids` / `hvx_mv_id` already skipped `-1`, `zero_skipped_dst_rows` writes 0 |
| zendnn | `mul_mat_id` | Real skip | slot dropped from the grouping loop, dst row memset |
| ggml-et | `mul_mat_id_*` kernels | No work saved (already correct) | already wrote 0 for out-of-range ids before this change; the kernel is per-output-element, so nothing is wasted either |
| **CANN** | `ggml_cann_mul_mat_id_fp` / `_quant` | **NOT IMPLEMENTED** | uses `aclnn IndexSelect` with the ids verbatim; a negative index is invalid |
| **OpenVINO** | `translate_mul_mat_id` | **NOT IMPLEMENTED** | uses `ov::op::Gather`, where a negative index means "from the end" -> silently picks the wrong expert |
| RPC | passthrough | n/a | forwards to the remote backend |

title: CUDA: FA support for head size 192/128 with GQA ratios that are not a multiples of 8.
body:
## Overview

The 192, 128 Flash Attention kernels currently require the GQA ratio to be a multiple of 8. Motif 3 #26298 uses the same head sizes with a GQA ratio of 5, so Flash attention is currently unavailable for it.

As far as I can tell the MMA kernel already supports partially filled GQA tiles. The launcher ceil divides the GQA dimension, out of bound channels are zero filled on Q load, and are skipped on write back, and the stream k fixup kernels also have the same bounds check.  

The gqa_ratio % 8 == 0 assert was stricter than the kernel requires. This PR relaxes that check to allow arbitary GQA ratios for (192, 128) via partially filled 8 channel tiles, gated on turing_mma_availabe since the generic tile kernel has no similar channel masking, and must not be selected for these shapes. So devices without  turing_mma_availabe fall back to BEST_FATTN_KERNEL_NONE as before. 

Also adds nr2 == 5 FLASH_ATTN_EXT cases (hsk 192 only) to test backend ops.

Test backend ops -o FLASH_ATTN_EXT passes on RTX 5090, and end to end generation with Motif 3 Beta at Q5_K_M is coherent, and behaves as expected with -fa on. On gpu's with turing_mma_available -fa auto now enables FA when using Motif 3.

title: rpc: include nb in the get_alloc_size cache key and floor the result at ggml_nbytes
body:
Hey there! 


## Overview

I am fairly new to this codebase, so please do let me know if I am barking up the wrong tree here; I encountered allocation issues with my local RPC setup and think I've chased this down to this nb include issue.

error occurs at `ggml-alloc.c:607, GGML_ASSERT(parent_size >= node_size), exit 134. R`

I've added nb to the cache key and never return less than ggml_nbytes. 

- rpc_tensor already carries nb, RPC_PROTO_* is untouched, #24292 stays the API  shouldn't change, so I think we're still good here. 
- I see @rgerganov 30–70 % PP from the memo; AFAICT, the contiguous tensors still hit the cache exactly as before, since their nb is a function of ne.
- I've read through #18626 and the note that the cache could be improved in follow-ups; I hope this counts!


## Additional information

Currently, the memo added in #18626 keys RPC_CMD_GET_ALLOC_SIZE results on {device, type, op, op_params, ne} and leaves nb out.

Two tensors with identical ne but different strides therefore share one entry, and the second caller receives the first tensor's size. When that size is smaller than ggml_nbytes, the buffer-type contract documented in #27960 and #28038 is violated and allocation fails downstream.


I've reproduced against a local ggml-rpc-server -d CPU: a packed tensor reports 16384/16384 and a strided view with the same ne reports nbytes 32512, alloc_size 16384, then aborts; with this change the second call reports 32512 and the run completes. The regression is folded into tests/test-rpc-multi-server.

body:
## Overview
In current PR introduced `--repack` option in llama-bench tool, which eliminates gap between this tool and `llama-cli`. It makes tool usage more flexible for multiple backends.
Initial problem was: llama-bench has no option to switch between code branches, while  `llama-cli` has.
In llama.cpp there always was a dedicated runtime knob to control compute code path (use_extra_bufts from llama_model_params). There were no command line option to set it in runtime exactly ,because it parses args in its own parse_cmd_params() rather than through common/arg.cpp . So current PR  only expose already available in engine capability to llama-bench tool. 

## Additional information
Once I was working with `llama-bench` and `llama-cli` tools, I have faced with lack of valuable (based on my opinion) option in `llama-bench`, but available in `llama-cli`. `--repack` allows to switch compute code branches and it might be useful for performance comparison for full picture of performance on HW understanding.
I have verified that neither LLAMA_ARG_REPACK nor -ot ".*=CPU"  can control it on runtime. The only option is to switch it in compile time -DGGML_CPU_REPACK=OFF.
Current option is valid at least for x86 and ARM CPUs

title: server: fix router eviction races with the existing queue
body:
## Overview

Minimal fix for #28698 A+B repro script, one commit per variant, reusing the existing scheduler queue instead of adding a new reservation mechanism.

A) A model loaded by the fast path has no queue entry, so tick() evicts it at its LOADED transition before its own request is proxied. Every load now goes through the queue, whose entry already protects a loading model from eviction until its waiters leave.

B) A request for a model that is being stopped still sees it LOADED and is proxied into the dying child. Such a request now joins the queue and is served by the next instance, and the stopping mark is cleared under the same lock that sets UNLOADED.

The full server test suite passes locally.

## Additional information

title: server: return prompt-token logprobs when echo=true (#27174)
body:
## Overview

Fixes #27174.

This PR enables support for `echo=true` combined with `logprobs=N` in the `/v1/completions` endpoint without triggering memory assertions or KV cache errors. Previously, the server ignored the `echo` setting for logprobs, returning an empty list for prompt tokens and breaking downstream evaluation frameworks like `lm-eval`.

## Additional information

### Motivation
Evaluation frameworks like `lm-eval` grade a model by feeding it a specific correct answer as a prompt and adding up the logprobs for those prompt tokens to calculate a total score[cite: 1]. Because prompt scores were missing, `lm-eval` received blanks and assumed the model was randomly guessing[cite: 1]. Furthermore, naive attempts to fix this caused a `GGML_ASSERT(n_outputs_max <= cparams.n_outputs_max)` hard abort on large prompts due to buffer overflow.

### Changes
* **Dynamic Capacity Query**: Expose `llama_n_outputs_max` in the core API (`include/llama.h` and `src/llama-context.cpp`) to safely query runtime output capacity.
* **Main Loop Chunking**: Integrate chunked prompt logprob extraction directly into the main prompt processing loop in `tools/server/server-context.cpp`.
* **Memory and Cache Safety**: Bound prompt token ingestion per iteration by `llama_n_outputs_max(ctx_tgt)` when `need_prompt_logits()` is true. This prevents output buffer overflow (fixing the hard abort) and ensures the KV cache timeline advances consecutively (fixing sequence inconsistency errors).
* **Zero VRAM Bloat**: Extract logprobs within existing memory limits without requiring extra startup VRAM allocation.
* **OAI JSON Formatting**: Correctly populate `token_logprobs` and `top_logprobs` for the echoed prompt tokens, ensuring the first prompt token explicitly returns `null`.

## Requirements

- Row reorder (in_proj_*): permute B rows

body:
## Overview

Backend sampler capability checks currently use a fixed candidate count when probing backend support. This may reject valid backend configurations for models with smaller vocabularies.

This change makes sampler probing shape-aware by using the actual model vocabulary size when evaluating backend support.

## Additional information

The sampler currently checks backend support using a hardcoded candidate count of 1024 * 1024. Since models can have different vocabulary sizes, this can incorrectly reject valid TOP_K configurations. 

**Motivation**: This issue was identified while enabling TOP_K support for the Hexagon backend (PR #29113). Model vocabularies such as Qwen (~152K) and Gemma (~262K) are significantly smaller than the probe size, which can incorrectly reject otherwise supported configurations. The sampler now uses the model vocabulary size during backend capability probing.

title: model : add DeepSeek V4.1 (DeepseekV41ForCausalLM)
body:
## Overview

Adds DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (`DeepseekV41ForCausalLM`) under its own `deepseek41` architecture: conversion, the runtime graph, and the chat template. An earlier revision of this PR was conversion only, so a converted file had nowhere to load. It is now the full path.

16 commits, 23 files, +2090 / -77.

### Conversion

Subclasses the existing V4 model. Most of the V4 path carries over unchanged. What needed handling:

- Text parameters are nested under `text_config`, so they are promoted in `index_tensors`. Overriding `load_hparams` does not work, because `ModelBase.__init__` calls it explicitly rather than through the instance.
- `num_hash_layers` is absent in V4.1 while the V4 path reads it unconditionally.
- The FP8 scale block size is `[32, 32]` rather than `[128, 128]`. V4 hardcodes 128, and reusing that value rescales every dequantized weight without raising, so the block size is read from `quantization_config`.
- Indexer `k_norm` and `wk` map onto the existing `INDEXER_K_NORM` and `INDEXER_ATTN_K`. `attn.compressor.ape` and `attn.indexer.compressor.*` are absent in V4.1 and go unused.
- Four new tensors for the engram conditional memory (`ENGRAM_EMBD`, `ENGRAM_Q`, `ENGRAM_K`, `ENGRAM_WKV`).

The two engram tables need a separate write path. Each is `384,006,168 x 256`, and the inherited FP8 dequant computes `weight.float() * scale` over the whole tensor, which is about 393 GB as float32 for one table. They are read in row blocks from the safetensors shard, quantized per block, and accumulated into a disk backed memmap. Their scale layout also differs: `[rows, 8]`, one scale per 32 columns of a single row, rather than the `[rows/32, cols/32]` tiling the linear weights use.

### Runtime

`src/models/deepseek41.cpp` is the V4.1 graph. Three things are not V4, and two of them fail silently rather than raising:

- **Sparse attention.** V4 keys everything off `dsv4_compress_ratios[il]` being 4 or 128. In the released V4.1 checkpoint those ratios are 0, 1 and 2, so V4's builder matches neither branch and drops the long range half of attention while still producing fluent text. V4.1 puts compressors on a few source layers rather than every layer, applies a pooling gate only where the ratio is above 1, and takes index keys from the shared KV latent through `indexer.wk` and `k_norm` rather than a second compressor. Nothing here is hardcoded: the loader derives each layer's role from which tensors the file actually carries, since only a compressor owner has the compressor weights, only an index key owner carries `indexer_attn_k`, and only an index source carries `indexer_attn_q_b`.
- **No q head norm.** V4 applies an extra unweighted `rms_norm` to `q` after `wq_b`. V4.1 does not. Also silent: the output stays fluent and is wrong.
- **Engram.** Two tables, on layers 1 and 14, with different row counts (384,006,168 and 384,016,682) because each layer seeds its own prime sized buckets. The lookup is a prime modulo hash reading `(max_ngram_size - 1) * n_heads = 24` rows per token per engram layer, so 48 per token, every token. The tables want to be host resident rather than treated as ordinary weights.

The compressed stream helpers in `llama_kv_cache_dsv4` are shared with V4 rather than duplicated, which is most of the diff to `src/llama-kv-cache-dsv4.cpp` and `src/models/deepseek4.cpp`.

This path also exposed an upstream bug, fixed here: `llama_kv_cache::build_input_k_rot` loops forever when `n_embd_head_k_all` is 0, which is what a cache whose layer filter selected nothing leaves it at. It presents as a hang at 100% of one core in `graph_reserve` with no error. V4 never hits it because its compressed caches always have layers.

## The architecture name

An earlier revision of this PR rode on `MODEL_ARCH.DEEPSEEK4` and added the engram tensors to V4's own list. That was wrong twice over, and it now declares `deepseek41` instead. `DEEPSEEK4` is left untouched.

**Convention.** llama.cpp does not mirror the HF `model_type`, it drops the `_v`: `deepseek_v2` became `deepseek2`, `deepseek_v3.2` became `deepseek32`, `qwen2_moe` became `qwen2moe`. Only 11 of the 153 arch strings in `constants.py` contain an underscore at all, so vLLM's `deepseek_v41` would be the odd one out here.

**Failure mode.** V4.1 ships the per-layer `hc_attn_{fn,base,scale}` and `hc_ffn_{fn,base,scale}`, 40 of each, but none of `output_hc_fn`, `output_hc_base` or `output_hc_scale`. Routing a V4.1 file to the V4 loader therefore produces a confusing partial match rather than a clean refusal. The declared lists show the same thing: `DEEPSEEK4` carries 48 tensor families and `deepseek41` carries 39, and the 15 it does not use include all three `HC_HEAD_*` and all six `NEXTN_*`.

`deepseek41`'s tensor list is the 39 families the converter actually writes, derived by reverse mapping them through `TENSOR_NAMES` rather than by trimming V4's list. Against `DEEPSEEK4` it drops `HC_HEAD_{FN,BASE,SCALE}`, `FFN_GATE_TID2EID`, `ATTN_COMPRESSOR_APE`, the four `INDEXER_COMPRESSOR_*` and all six `NEXTN_*`, and adds six: the four `ENGRAM_*` plus `INDEXER_ATTN_K` and `INDEXER_K_NORM`.

## Additional information

**Conversion.** Converted `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` end to end on one machine with 121 GiB of RAM: 1046 tensors, 507.9 GB at `--outtype q8_0` with MXFP4 experts, peak host memory under 8 GB above baseline. Output checked with `GGUFReader`, all 8 engram tensors present. Quantized further to Q2_K and Q3_K_M to confirm the file is well formed downstream.

Measured rung sizes, for anyone estimating: Q8_0 staging 473.1 GiB (1046 tensors), Q2_K 246.3 GiB, Q3_K_M 323.4 GiB. Those ratios read high against the staging file because it is not uniformly Q8_0: routed experts land as MXFP4, so parts of the ladder move up rather than down. At Q3_K_M the expert down projection goes MXFP4 to q5_K and grows from 2295 to 2970 MiB.

`Q2_K_S` and `IQ2_M` both need an imatrix. Q1_0 is unusable on this model and it is the file rather than the runtime: a 1 bit block format leaves the token embedding table as plus or minus a single magnitude per row, and the embedding is the only place prompt identity enters the model, so every prompt returns the same token. Q2_K is the first usable rung.

**Runtime.** Runs at Q2_K on a DGX Spark (GB10, 128 GB unified memory) at 2.8 tok/s with GPU offload and 2.3 without, coherent and on topic. The serve line that works there:

```
-lm mmap -ngl 99 -cmoe -ot "engram_embd.weight=CPU" -fa on -c 2048 -b 2048 -ub 1024 -t 20
```

`-lm mmap` is required on that box for any model larger than RAM. The default `auto` disables mmap globally if any device reports no mmap support, and the GB10 CUDA device reports exactly that, after which a 246 GB model tries to allocate 261 GB up front.

**Build and tests.** `llama`, `common` and `test-chat` all compile against current master, and `test-chat` passes.

**Not in this PR.** Three commits improving `q1_0` (imatrix block scale, a mixed precision recipe, token embedding promotion) were dropped from this branch. They are general quantization changes rather than V4.1 work and belong in their own PR.

**Credit.** Three of the commits here are @midagedev's, carried with authorship intact: the DSpark draft path in `src/models/dflash.cpp` so a V4.1 draft without the `output_hc_*` head loads, `n_swa = 0` so `llama-server` keeps its checkpoints, and the V4.1 DSML tag names with a jinja template and its tests. V4.1 renamed those tags to a leading space form (`" calls"`, `" invoke"`, `" parameter"`) and the converted file was carrying the V4 template.

Thanks also to @RefractAI, @drrros, @smalinin, @ThinkOffApp and @darth-veitcher for review and testing on the thread, and to @JigSawPT, whose independent port found the missing q head norm separately.

title: hip : skip fully masked KV tiles in WMMA Flash Attention
body:
## What changed

When server slots share a unified KV cache, the AMD WMMA Flash Attention kernel can still compute interior KV tiles that are fully masked for the current request. Following the review suggestion, this revision moves mask scanning and reduction out of the attention loop and into an auxiliary preprocessing kernel.

The new flash_attn_mask_to_KV_blocks classifies each block as fully masked, all-zero, or general. The attention kernel skips runs of fully masked blocks, omits mask loading and mask addition for all-zero runs, and keeps normal mask evaluation for general blocks. Sixteen two-bit classes pack into a single 32-bit word and are reused across attention heads.

This path is limited to synchronous, dense AMD WMMA. It covers the measured -ub 512 --kv-unified configuration, in which the existing flash_attn_mask_to_KV_max helper is not launched. The patch also includes the broadcast-mask and query-tail fixes plus additional operator tests.


On RX 7900 XTX / Ubuntu 24.04 / ROCm 7.2.1, third-request time drops by approximately 33.3% versus upstream, and by a further 10% versus V1. The gain is primarily in prefill; this is not a general decode or concurrent-server throughput claim.

The model is Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M, fully offloaded, with Flash Attention enabled. The workload uses 98,304 context capacity, 40,960 input / 64 output tokens, and two unified-cache slots requested sequentially in 0/1/0 order. Ubatch is 512, with no prompt cache reuse and no speculative decoding.

| KV cache | Upstream | V2 | 95% CI for relative time change, V2 vs upstream |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| F16 | 77.8 s | 51.9 s | [-33.447%, -33.225%] |
| Q8_0 | 80.3 s | 53.5 s | [-33.330%, -33.257%] |

Times are geometric means over six restarts per variant, covering all six U/V1/V2 execution orders on the common base c6824a9. Confidence intervals use paired log-ratios. The current source is ported to ec91ab5; the three-arm performance comparison has not been repeated on that base.

## Validation

- **Operator tests on ec91:** 4,007 passed, 0 failed, 1,323 unsupported. The extended suite adds boundary cases. Upstream and V1 each fail six of the new broadcast-mask cases that V2 fixes; these are not failures in pre-existing upstream CI tests.
- **Model checks:** fixed F16/Q8_0 perplexity matches the per-chunk reference values at printed precision, without claiming bitwise-identical internals. Sequential requests match the reference token IDs.
- **Kernel trace:** all 3,840 WMMA calls in the instrumented run had a preceding classifier launch on the same stream. Peak dispatch metadata was 5,184 bytes; this is not total extra VRAM.
- **Local HIP CI:** passed in aggregate, after one HTTP-test failure was re-run and passed and the model-download interruptions were resolved. This was not an uninterrupted all-green run. The full operator suite also relied on a separate TOPK comparator fix, which is excluded from this attention patch.


The [V2 evidence release](https://github.com/moristeven477-ship-it/llama.cpp/releases/tag/rdna3-masked-kv-v2-20260921) contains the patch, commands, hashes, raw data, and logs. The V1 artifacts do not substitute for this evidence.

- [V2 patch on ec91](https://github.com/moristeven477-ship-it/llama.cpp/releases/download/rdna3-masked-kv-v2-20260921/attention-v2-ec91.patch); [SHA256 checksums](https://github.com/moristeven477-ship-it/llama.cpp/releases/download/rdna3-masked-kv-v2-20260921/SHA256SUMS).
- Reproduction commands: [c682 performance](https://github.com/moristeven477-ship-it/llama.cpp/releases/download/rdna3-masked-kv-v2-20260921/REPRODUCE-c682.md) / [ec91 validation](https://github.com/moristeven477-ship-it/llama.cpp/releases/download/rdna3-masked-kv-v2-20260921/REPRODUCE-ec91.md).
- [Raw performance data](https://github.com/moristeven477-ship-it/llama.cpp/releases/download/rdna3-masked-kv-v2-20260921/p23-primary-native-20260920.tar.gz) and [primary-workload findings](https://github.com/moristeven477-ship-it/llama.cpp/releases/download/rdna3-masked-kv-v2-20260921/primary-FINDINGS.zh.md).
- [CI and model logs](https://github.com/moristeven477-ship-it/llama.cpp/releases/download/rdna3-masked-kv-v2-20260921/p23-ec91-ci-and-models-20260921.tar.gz), plus [CI scope](https://github.com/moristeven477-ship-it/llama.cpp/releases/download/rdna3-masked-kv-v2-20260921/ci-FINDINGS.zh.md).
- [Matched operator tests, calibration, and raw kernel traces](https://github.com/moristeven477-ship-it/llama.cpp/releases/download/rdna3-masked-kv-v2-20260921/p23-ec91-final-evidence-20260921.tar.gz).

## Credit & inspiration

Thanks to JohannesGaessler for the auxiliary-preprocessing suggestion, to DanoPTT for the V1 testing and the helper-launch diagnosis, and to alankila together with the earlier reports in #28495 and #14924. The masked-block preprocessing idea follows other backends, including Vulkan (#17186); the ec91 port retains ynankani's swizzle work (#28536).

title: Expert Caching that can boost performance, heatmap, mmap pinning based on heatmap, real time cpu to device transfer and device to cpu transfer. Fully conditional on flags and self contained to not affect execution path outside of them
body:
This is the successor to https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/26563
People seem to want full performance, and other options I had not initially included. If a reviewer wants me to remove features, or apply some more "hacky"fixes and make a smaller diff version or a cleaner commit history, I am very willing to do both 

## Additions:

0. Everything is dependent on flags. The process without any of the flags active is simply a 1:1 original llama instance. I did not change defaults or make anything non opt-in
1. 2 different configurable ways to feed the heat-map with decay, from the cold path counts or from graph readback so it also works standalone
2. Expert-level offload granularity, so the store splits the MoE weights per expert instead of per layer
3. Device priority stores based on heatmap, so the hottest experts go to the best device and colder ones spill down to the weaker ones
4. Expert pinning and evicting on mmap, so the pages of stable GPU experts get dropped while the likely-next ones stay warm and evictions never refault from disk
5. Custom ram pool with reduced ram usage when -no-mmap is run along with multiple devices, since the expert tensors get ghost buffers and only what the cpu path needs is actually held
6. Auto-fit on new functionality (off by default, ehs -1 activates everything. Slots into existing autofit so that has to be enabled or the slots set manually)
7. Respects -ts and splits the expert slots according to it
8. Separate throttled pcie to pcie device queue to reduce thrashing on multi gpu, with one move per turn and per-pair scratch buffers
9. Multiple debug dials, examples of which include printing the heatmap every time stats print
10. May work in multiple backends (I have seen others confirm but can only verify myself on vulkan and cuda)
11. Fused cold op path, so the cold experts are calculated in one pass instead of three separate ones
12. Copy or move mode, since copying the experts to the gpu costs ram while moving frees the ram after a verified transfer
13. Verified swap handshake, since every expert move is hash verified before it is routed so corruption from torn copies is not a thing
14. Sidecar heatmap persistence, so the heatmap is saved to a file next to the model on exit and loaded on the next launch so the store starts already converged
15. Hit-rate driven adaptive resync cadence, so the swap period grows the longer the store proves itself stable and a settled store barely re-plans
16. Set Device GPU store and priority manually (currently follows default device priority, may add manual switch too if people want it)

## Quick start:
Use -ehs N to set number of expert slots. Never use in conjunction with -ncmoe as that takes away vram for static experts. In most cases its recommended to just set fit target. Otherwise you'll have to figure out the best value to set.
copy vs move mode.
Copy mode stores all experts on system RAM and only copies them over to vram. Takes up more RAM, but is faster to heat up
Move mode only keeps 1 copy of an expert at a time, moving them between your cpu and gpu. When run with -no-mmap (you cant copy experts back to mmap), it saves ram but slower to heat up
-expert-sidecar saves your heatmap next to your model file on exit or loads a previously saved heatmap if present. Helps a lot with initial speed.
-expert-pin N. Pins the N% of hottest experts on your mmap to your ram using willneed. early testing shows the optimal value is between 30 and 60 depending on model size. You can do 100 if you want to use heatmap but the model fits so you just want to have it set all memory as willneed. However pinning on its own has shown minimal benefit especially on well optimized linux distros.

## Who is this for?:
Everyone can test it, but most benefit will be visible to people with 1 gpu, who have a model they can fit at least 40% of the model in their vram. Configurations outside of that can also provide a benefit but it can be hit or miss.

## Known limitations:
Multi gpu performance. I have designed a swap system that in theory should not have overhead. However, I lack proper testing apparatus so multi gpu performance may not be optimal
Back-end support: Others have reported past versions working on other back-ends too. I hope thats the case. However, i am not rich. I only have access to 2 GPUs one of which is Vulcan only and old. So i can only test on Vulcan and CUDA.
Due to differences in floating point calculations depending on where each expert is calculated, even at temp 0, when different experts are cached, the output may slightly vary. I have run extended tests and confirmed this is not silent corruption and happens on the original llama too if you change "--n-cpu-moe"
High end hardware. I do not have access to any. So its impossible to optimise. Some have reported good results, some bad. But I would need to work closer with people to understand
Under 256 token generation sessions: When llama.cpp itself (client, server, etc) has processed less than 256 tokens it may be slower than stock. If you do not close and re open the client it will quickly start outpacing it. Benchmarks that generate 128 tokens and restart the server will produce uncharacteristically bad results that are not representative of real world performance.
While -np2 works, the slowdown will be bigger than on stock. So its probably better for -np 1, about on par with -np 2, and worse after that.

## Warnings:
Auto-fit. Relies on stock autofit. If you have manually set -cmoe, -ncmoe, -ngl, etc etc, it will fail and you will have to manually submit a -ehs value.
If your cpu or PCI express buss is your bottleneck, it may worsen performance
The flags equivalent of -no-mmap uses a bit more ram than no mmap on the same configuration on stock (without the flags, or the pull request) due to the need for a buffer to move experts around without overwriting each other. I designed it so it only has a buffer on the CPU side so vram usage would not increase. The increase should be minor in most cases but worth knowing about
Full model fit: If the full model fits in your vram, this will purely cause slowdowns as it adds more cpu synchronization overhead. However if only 80% of the model fits, this may be the single biggest upgrade you could find.
Performance may be worse on vulkan or other back ends.

## Things I have talked about but were excluded for this commit but can plug into existing system: 
Semantic permanent heat maps + prefetch. Could be added in a future commit but is too big of a feature to include along with the rest here
Would benefit the most: People who want to use models drastically larger than their combined Ram.
Next expert predictive prefetch. It can actually cause a slowdown fow smaller models but for huge ones, it can be very beneficial.
For people who really want this: I hear you, I will be researching for the best way to do this with the least rewriting of original llama code over the next month

## Full technical explanation: 
Coming soon, I will go to sleep now. Excuse me for any possible multi hour delays in my responses.


## Benchmark methodology:

Prompt: Give me a guide on how to set up a Linux computer averaged over 3 runs of each (the deviation was within 5% so i wont be putting them individually to increase readability)
The sidecar test was run having pre warmed a sidecar with the phrase "Hello" over 128 tokens. Sidecars that were generated over longer periods will perform significantly better especially when there is topic overlap.
The only launch argument for both was -fitt 64 + -ehs -1 for mine.
Hardware: 8gb laptop 3070 + 32 GB of ram + laptop ssd. System conditions identical with all other processes ended.
I initially did multiple runs on stock, but realized it made no difference (within 1-2% regardless of token length), so i stuck with 1.

##Benchmark Results (short)

Model | Size | S | Stock (tok/s) | Request (tok/s) | Ratio
------|------|---|---------------|-----------------|-------
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (IQ2_M) | 12 GB | autofit | 38.1 | 59.7 | 1.57x |
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (Q4_K_M) | 21 GB | autofit | 32.0 | 47.7 | 1.49x 
Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-REAP-30 (IQ2_M) | 29 GB | autofit | 7.18 | 12.5 | 1.74x 
Gemma-4-26B-A4B (Q5_K_S) | 18 GB | autofit | 19.9 | 43.6 | 2.19x 
Laguna-S-2.1 (IQ3_XXS) | 44 GB | autofit | 2.01 | 2.05 | 1.02x |

## Benchmark results (detailed)

| model | config | 256 | 768 | 1792 | 3840 |
|-------|--------|-----|-----|------|------|
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B IQ2_M | stock | - | 38.1 | - | - |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B IQ2_M | tier | 34.8 | 47.4 | 59.5 | 59.7 |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B IQ2_M | sidecar | - | 44.2 | - | - |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q4_K_M | stock | - | 32.0 | - | - |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q4_K_M | tier | 33.8 | 43.3 | 47.7 | 43.7 |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q4_K_M | sidecar | - | 35.8 | - | - |
| Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-REAP-30 IQ2_M | stock | - | 7.18 | - | - |
| Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-REAP-30 IQ2_M | tier | 10.1 | 11.9 | 12.4 | 12.5 |
| Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-REAP-30 IQ2_M | sidecar | - | 8.71 | - | - |
| gemma-4-26B-A4B Q5_K_S | stock | - | 19.9 | - | - |
| gemma-4-26B-A4B Q5_K_S | tier | - | 36.2 | 42.0 | 43.6 |
| Laguna-S-2.1 IQ3_XXS | stock | - | 2.01 | - | - |
| Laguna-S-2.1 IQ3_XXS | tier | 1.66 | - | 2.05 | - |

These are not performance numbers under ideal conditions. What I did was run stock first, and others later, with clearing my rams cache fully in between. The late runs, which were always the tiered runs are thermally throttled. Under ideal conditions performance is 20% higher when not ram limited.

Note: It appears to be building normally on everything. But if someone encounters a platform specific error, I'll make sure to have it fixed by tomorrow. In the meantime you can get one of the pre made builds: https://github.com/miltos22/llama.cpp-wackMall-merge-request/actions/runs/31344712283#artifacts

title: CUDA: fix IQ1_S/IQ2_S/IQ3_S garbage output on Blackwell (sm_120)
body:
## Overview

The IQ1_S, IQ2_S, and IQ3_S MMQ tile-load and vec_dot kernels extract individual bytes from a packed 32-bit quant word by casting it to a uint8_t* and indexing (e.g. `qs[l]`). On nvcc 13.2 targeting sm_120 this byte read is miscompiled: the plain byte mask is dropped and the grid table index runs out of range, producing essentially random dequantized values. The result is coherent-looking output on very short prompts and garbage on anything longer. Both the MMQ path and the cuBLAS/dp4a vec_dot path are affected, so GGML_CUDA_FORCE_CUBLAS=1 does not help.

Replace the uint8_t* byte indexing with an explicit __byte_perm() byte selection, which forces correct codegen. Sibling types (IQ3_XXS, IQ4_XS, IQ2_XS, IQ2_XXS, K-quants) were already correct and are unchanged.

Fixes the 6 affected sites:
mmq-load-tiles.cuh: load_tiles_iq1_s / iq2_s / iq3_s vecdotq.cuh: vec_dot_iq1_s_q8_1 / iq2_s_q8_1 / iq3_s_q8_1


## Additional information

Verified on RTX 5060 Ti (sm_120, CUDA 13.2, driver 580.173.02): test-backend-ops -o MUL_MAT and -o MUL_MAT_ID now report OK for iq1_s/iq2_s/iq3_s (previously FAIL with NMSE ~0.2-1.1).

Fixes #28581

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)

title: ui : fix missing svg use and animation elements in preview and download
body:
## Overview

Fixes #28336

When the model outputs SVG graphics that utilize structural reuse (`<use href="#id"/>`) or declarative animations (`<animate>`, `<set>`), elements are missing or static in both the rendered preview and downloaded SVG file.

While `SVG.SOURCE_ATTR` retains the complete raw markup (so "Copy" works), the preview and download pathways run through DOMPurify with `USE_PROFILES: { svg: true, svgFilters: true }`. DOMPurify's default SVG profile omits `<use>`, `<animate>`, and `<set>`, as well as interpolation attributes `from`, `to`, and `calcMode`.

### Solution
  - Extend `SVG.SANITIZE_CONFIG` with:
  - `ADD_TAGS: ['animate', 'set', 'use']`
  - `ADD_ATTR: ['calcMode', 'from', 'to']`
  - Fulfills the original intent noted in `svg-blocks.constants.ts` ("href and xlink:href stay so use, image, a and animateMotion work").

## Additional information
  - `<script>` and `<foreignObject>` remain forbidden under `FORBID_TAGS`.
  - URI attributes (`href`, `xlink:href`) continue to be sanitized against `javascript:` / `vbscript:` schemes.
  - All attributes matching `/^on/i` (event handlers) remain stripped.
  - All sanitized SVG output remains isolated within a browser Shadow Root.

## Requirements

title: vulkan: add Intel Xe flash attention optimization kernels (2/3, Xe-LPG Plus/Xe2/Xe3)
body:
## Overview

**Co-authors:** @jxia4intel, @sliu39

**PR 2/3** of the Intel Xe optimization series — see https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24408 (mega PR, draft) for the full feature set.

**Target platforms:** Xe-LPG Plus, Xe2, Xe3

This PR adds Intel Xe-specific flash attention optimization kernels for both ARLH iGPU (Xe1, UMA, coopmat1) and Xe2/Xe3. Dependency: builds on top of https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24404 (Xe-LPG Plus coopmat1 enable). Independent of https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24407 (GEMM+CW).

### Flash Attention (Intel Xe)

- New Vulkan shaders: single-phase prefill (`flash_attn_hdim64/96/128`) and two-phase split prefill/decode variants
- Pipelines keyed by `(head_dim, gqa_ratio)` for runtime dispatch across various GQA ratios without combinatorial pipeline proliferation
- Supports non-power-of-two GQA ratios via subgroup splitting (`qk_groups`)
- Intel Xe1 (integrated GPU, UMA, cooperative matrix) and Xe2 paths with separate warptile tuning
- Two-phase decode splits softmax reduction across subgroups; shared QK state copy (`fa_copy_qstate`) between prefill phases

### Performance (Panther Lake B390 + Windows OS)

title: ggml : add PQ2_0 and PTQ1_0 ternary types; llama : apply Hadamard-folded weights
body:
Adds support for the ternary GGUFs published as
[prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf](https://huggingface.co/prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf)
(Apache-2.0, 27B, `qwen35`). Two things are missing today, and both are needed: the tensor
types, and the activation-side transform for weights that are stored folded into a rotated basis.

Requested in #29058. Today such a file either fails to parse ("the type ids sit past
`GGML_TYPE_COUNT`") or, when the type is one llama.cpp already knows (`Q2_0`), loads without a
warning and produces incoherent text, because no mainline runtime applies the rotation declared in
the file's metadata.

## What is in here

**1. The two tensor types** (`ggml`)

| type | id | group | block | layout |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `PQ2_0` | 142 | 128 | 34 B | fp16 scale + each trit in a 2-bit slot, same codec as `Q2_0` |
| `PTQ1_0` | 143 | 128 | 28 B | fp16 scale + dense base-3 trits (5/byte, remainder at 4/byte), as in `TQ1_0` |

They are group-128 variants of `Q2_0`/`TQ1_0`, so the reference quantizers/dequantizers are ports of
the existing ones with the group size changed. The ids are deliberately high: the published files
already carry 142/143, and matching them is the only way to read those artifacts.

CPU wiring: `from_float` (reference quantizer), `to_float`, `vec_dot_type = Q8_0`, and a `vec_dot`.
The `vec_dot` here is a **reference kernel** — dequantize the block, accumulate in F32 — which is
correct but slow (~0.4 tok/s for the 27B on 16 threads). SIMD paths for `ggml-cpu` are a deliberate
follow-up, together with the GPU backends (see below).

**2. The folded-weight runtime** (`llama`)

`prism.hadamard.*` metadata describes weights stored as `W'` with the model defined as
`y = W' * (H * (s * P * x))`, where `H` is a normalized Sylvester-Hadamard matrix applied in blocks of
`block_size` along the input axis, `s` a per-input-width sign vector, and `P` an optional feature
permutation for the grouped GDN path. The metadata is self-describing and is validated before it is
trusted:

- version, block size (power of two, must divide every named weight's input dimension), transform and
  axis names, sign mode, and non-empty weight list;
- explicit sign mode must supply widths whose lengths sum exactly to the sign-value count, and every
  value must be `+1`/`-1`;
- only architectures whose matmuls are all routed through `build_lora_mm`/`build_lora_mm_id` are
  accepted (`llama`, `qwen3`, `qwen3moe`, `qwen35`, `qwen35moe`, `qwen3next`), and only tensor kinds
  verified to be on those paths may be folded. Anything else throws instead of running wrong math;
- the inverse path is limited to `token_embd.weight`, which is the only row-lookup table the graph
  restores (`h = s * (H z)` after the lookup).

One rotation matrix is built per (block size, buffer type) and one sign vector per input width, both
as persistent model tensors; the per-weight association lives in the model and reaches the graph
through `llm_graph_params`. Transformations on the same activation are memoized per graph build so
weights sharing an activation do not each rebuild one.

This reuses what already exists upstream: `llama_mul_mat_hadamard` and the `GGML_HINT_SRC0_IS_HADAMARD`
hint, the FWHT kernels, and the same "one cached rotation matrix per shape" pattern as the attention
KV-rotation feature.

## Verification

- **Numerical equivalence with the reference implementation.** Perplexity on
  `wikitext-2-raw/wiki.test.raw`, `-c 64 --chunks 2`: this branch gives
  **PPL = 16.2538** and Prism's fork built from the same tag gives **16.2588** — a 0.03% difference,
  consistent with this branch dequantizing to F32 while the fork uses Q8 dot kernels. If the transform
  were wrong or missing, the number is nonsense rather than 0.03% off.
- `tests/test-quantize-fns` passes for both new types (the ternary thresholds in that test now include
  them; without that entry the types are judged against the default threshold).
- `llama-cli` loads the 27B PQ2_0 file, and `llama-bench` runs it (`pp8`/`tg1`, CPU only).

## Not in here

- **GPU kernels.** CUDA/Metal/Vulkan/SYCL have no `PQ2_0`/`PTQ1_0` support in this PR, so the types
  fall back to CPU there. Porting the fork's kernels is the next step and is what makes these packs
  practical (the same 27B runs at ~135 tok/s on an RTX 5090 with them).
- **Fast CPU kernels** (repack, SIMD `vec_dot`).
- `LLAMA_FTYPE_MOSTLY_PQ2_0`/`PTQ1_0` and quantize-tool support: the published files report
  `general.file_type` 141/143, which currently maps to "unknown" in the loader's log. Worth pinning
  down, but nothing depends on it yet.

## Testing notes

Built CPU-only with `cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=OFF -DLLAMA_CURL=OFF`, gcc in a container; the model
was loaded from the published pack (6.7 GiB, 402 `PQ2_0` tensors, 401 folded weights, 2 rotation
matrices and 3 sign vectors at block size 1024).

title: Force NVFP4 W4A8 path for NVFP4_W4A16 layers on Blackwell, where NVFP4 normally uses the native W4A4 path.
vulkan : copy strided f16 KV once on AMD so reads spread across memory channels
body:
## Overview

f16 KV layout does not engage all memory channels. This PR engages all channels by copying each layers f16 KV once into a scratch so that the KV cache reads are sequential. Reuse of scratch introduced in PR #25494 

## Additional information

<!-- You can provide more details and link related discussions here. Delete this section if not applicable -->
Gating set to AMD where effect was measured, RTX 3070 did not benefit, Intel and any other vendor have not been tested.

Consecutive KV rows of one head are read `n_kv_heads × head_dim × 2` bytes apart. Typical model KV geometry spacing is an even multiple of the 256B channel-interleave block that Mesa documents, causing only a subset of memory channels to engage. 
| KV geometry (heads × head_dim) | example models | row spacing | ÷ 256 B | channels engaged (of 16) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 × 128 | small GQA-heavy models | 512 B | 2 | 8 |
| 4 × 128 | Qwen3-Coder-30B *(benchmarked)* | 1024 B | 4 | 4 |
| 2 × 256 | Qwen3.6-35B class *(benchmarked)* | 1024 B | 4 | 4 |
| 4 × 256 | Qwen3.8-27B *(benchmarked)* | 2048 B | 8 | 2 |
| 8 × 128 | Llama-3.1-8B class | 2048 B | 8 | 2 |
| 32 × 128 | MHA-era 7B models | 8192 B | 32 | 1 |


The tradeoff is scratch size, 1 layer of KV
| KV geometry | example models | KV layers | scratch/token | @32k | @128k | % of f16 KV cache |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 × 128 | small GQA-heavy (typ. 32L) | 32 | 1 KiB | 32 MiB | 128 MiB | ~3.1% |
| 4 × 128 | Qwen3-Coder-30B *(measured)* | 48 | 2 KiB | 64 MiB | 256 MiB | 2.1% |
| 2 × 256 | Qwen3.6-35B (hybrid, 10/40 attn) | 10 | 2 KiB | 64 MiB | 256 MiB | 10% |
| 4 × 256 | Qwen3.8-27B (hybrid, 16/65 attn) | 16 | 4 KiB | 128 MiB | 512 MiB | 6.25% |
| 8 × 128 | Llama-3.1-8B class | 32 | 4 KiB | 128 MiB | 512 MiB | 3.1% |
| 32 × 128 | MHA-era 7B models | 32 | 16 KiB | 512 MiB | 2 GiB | 3.1% |


TG is measured unaffected, stridding tax increases at depth. Worst case model (hybrid, 10/40 attention layers) regress ~1% in prefill @ 32k, back within run variance @ 64k.

title: vulkan: make MMVQ row policies device-specific and tune NVIDIA MUL_MAT_ID
body:
## Overview

While profiling Vulkan MMVQ on NVIDIA, I found that row geometry has a significant impact on small-batch performance.

`rm_id` (`MUL_MAT_ID`) and `rm_int_n` (regular `MUL_MAT`) have different execution characteristics: regular `MUL_MAT` is more sensitive to column geometry, while `MUL_MAT_ID` has a less column-sensitive cost structure. The same pattern appears in the existing RDNA3 tuning in #27909, which uses a static 4-row `rm_id` policy but a column-dependent `rm_int_n` policy.

On the tested NVIDIA GPU, 4-row `MUL_MAT_ID` shows clear gains, while regular `MUL_MAT` remains strongly type- and shape-dependent.

This PR changes only the `rm_id` row policy: NVIDIA devices not classified as `NVIDIA_PRE_TURING` now use 4 rows. The shared RDNA3 predicate is expanded into the individual policy functions; RDNA3 behavior is unchanged, and regular `MUL_MAT` is not modified.

## Performance

Performance was measured on an RTX 5070 Ti 16 GB with locked clocks. Models were fully resident except for the explicitly marked Qwen3-30B case.

`llama-batched-bench` was run with the same batched setup as #27909 (`llama-batched-bench -npp 256 -ntg 256 -npl 1,2,4,8 -c 8192 -b 2048 -ub 512 -ngl 99`).

Positive values indicate throughput improvement relative to baseline.

| Workload / expert quantization            |    `npl=1` |    `npl=2` |     `npl=4` |         `npl=8` |
| ----------------------------------------- | ---------: | ---------: | ----------: | --------------: |
| Qwen3-16B-A3B legacy (`q4_0/q4_1/q5_0`)   | -3.7…-0.1% | +9.3…10.7% | +21.1…23.9% | **+31.7…37.6%** |
| Qwen3-16B-A3B Q3_K_M                      |      +2.1% |      +4.3% |       +8.7% |      **+14.7%** |
| Qwen3-16B-A3B Q2_K                        |      +2.4% |      +4.7% |       +4.7% |      **+11.7%** |
| DeepSeek-V2-Lite Q5_K_M                   |      -0.2% |      +6.6% |       +2.8% |      **+14.2%** |
| GPT-OSS-20B MXFP4                         |      +0.0% |      +1.0% |       +4.8% |       **+3.4%** |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B Q4_K_M (31% expert offload) |      -1.8% |      +0.0% |       +2.2% |       **+3.5%** |

The benefit is concentrated in the larger small-batch workloads, with `npl=8` showing the strongest improvement for most affected families. Legacy quants show the largest gains, while the tested K-quant workloads reach approximately 12–15% at `npl=8`. The partially offloaded 30B model also improves with 31% expert CPU offload.

At `npl=1`, the effect is small and mixed around zero. More substantial gains appear at higher parallelism, with `npl=8` generally showing the strongest improvement.

Separate `-ub 32` controls outside the affected small-batch path remain unchanged within noise.

## Backend-op performance

The performance effect is also visible directly in llama.cpp's backend-op tests.

Values are changes in `us/run` relative to baseline; negative values are faster (`m=768, k=2048`, except MXFP4 with `m=2880, k=2880`).

| `MUL_MAT_ID` type | Affected `rm_id` path at `n=4/8` |  `n=4` |  `n=8` | `n=32` |
| ----------------- | -------------------------------- | -----: | -----: | -----: |
| `q4_0`            | yes                              | -34.2% | -36.9% |  +4.2% |
| `q4_K`            | yes                              | -27.5% | -29.9% |  +2.3% |
| `q8_0`            | yes                              | -27.8% |  -7.1% |  +5.6% |
| `MXFP4`           | yes                              | -15.5% | -16.0% |      — |
| `q6_K`            | no                               |  +1.0% |  +1.8% |  +3.7% |
| `iq2_xs`          | no                               |  +0.7% |  +3.4% |  +3.7% |

`n=32` is above `mul_mat_vec_max_cols` (8) and serves as an out-of-path control, with only small changes observed. `test-backend-ops` has no `MUL_MAT_ID` cases for `n=2` or `n=3`; smaller end-to-end workloads are covered by the `llama-batched-bench` results above.

I also tested an RDNA3-like 4-row policy on regular `MUL_MAT`:

| regular `MUL_MAT` type |  `n=3` |  `n=5` |  `n=8` |
| ---------------------- | -----: | -----: | -----: |
| `q4_0`                 | -30.6% | -34.1% | -33.4% |
| `q3_K`                 | -24.5% | -33.4% | -21.0% |
| `q4_1`                 | -24.8% | -33.1% | -33.4% |
| `q2_K`                 | -14.2% | -16.3% | +22.9% |
| `MXFP4`                | -10.6% | -18.6% |  +9.7% |

On the tested NVIDIA GPU, the response is strongly type- and shape-dependent: several types benefit substantially from 4 rows, while others regress for some column counts. This does not support a single static 4-row policy for NVIDIA regular `MUL_MAT`, unlike the column-dependent RDNA3 policy from #27909.

This is consistent with the cost analysis: regular `MUL_MAT` temporary state grows with both `NUM_ROWS` and `NUM_COLS`, making its preferred row geometry more sensitive to column shape and device resource behavior.

For this reason, the only behavioral change in this PR is the NVIDIA `rm_id` policy; regular `MUL_MAT` tuning remains device-specific.

## Validation and scope

```text
test-backend-ops test -o MUL_MAT_ID

937/937 tests passed

test-backend-ops test -o MUL_MAT

1128/1128 tests passed
```

The performance change is limited to the expected small-batch `MUL_MAT_ID` region. `q6_K` is unchanged in normal NVIDIA execution, as expected: the current MMVQ selector rejects it before the `rm_id` geometry is used, so this change does not enable a previously disabled path.

The current performance characterization is limited to the tested RTX 5070 Ti / Blackwell device.

## Requirements

* I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md).
* AI usage disclosure: Yes, for issue analysis and writing code.

title: ggml-cpu : yield in ggml_barrier after a short spin
body:
## Overview

`ggml_barrier` waits with a pure `ggml_thread_cpu_relax()` spin. When there are more compute threads than cores, a thread spinning at a barrier burns its scheduler quantum while the thread it is waiting for cannot run, so every barrier costs scheduler round trips instead of nanoseconds and throughput collapses.

`test-thread-safety` hits this on 2-core hosts: 2 models × 4 contexts, each decoding with a 2-thread pool, is 16 compute threads on 2 cores. GitHub's standard Windows runners for **private** repositories have 2 vCPUs (public ones get 4), where the test hits the 900 s ctest timeout with no output after the contexts are created; upstream's 4-core runs take ~55 s. Downstream forks that run this CI privately see every Windows x64 job fail this way. Upstream's own Windows x64 jobs mostly avoid the code path since #26678 (fetched LLVM OpenMP, whose barrier yields), except `x64-openblas` which builds with `-DGGML_OPENMP=OFF` and only passes thanks to the 4 cores.

This change spins for `GGML_BARRIER_SPINS_BEFORE_YIELD` (2048) relax iterations, roughly 50–100 µs on x86, then calls `sched_yield()` between polls. The uncontended case, where the other threads arrive within microseconds, never reaches the yield.

## Measurements

`test-thread-safety` with its CI arguments (`-ngl 99 -n 128 -c 256 -ub 32 -np 4 -t N`), `GGML_OPENMP=OFF`, tinyllamas/stories15M-q4_0, all runs producing the same 8 completions:

| host | build | `-t 1` | `-t 2` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Linux, e2-standard-2 (2 vCPU) | pure spin | 1.9 s | **147 s** |
| Linux, e2-standard-2 (2 vCPU) | this PR | 1.8 s | **4.4 s** |
| Windows Server 2022, e2-standard-2 (2 vCPU), clang | pure spin | 5 s | **900 s timeout, 0/8 contexts** |
| Windows Server 2022, e2-standard-2 (2 vCPU), clang | this PR | 5 s | **7 s** |
| macOS M4 Pro (14 cores), `-np 4 -t 2` (uncontended) | pure spin | | 0.1 s |
| macOS M4 Pro (14 cores), `-np 4 -t 2` (uncontended) | this PR | | 0.1 s |

On the M4 Pro an oversubscribed run (`-np 8 -t 14`, 224 threads on 14 cores) with the pure spin had not finished after 40 minutes when I stopped it.

The secondary threads' `ggml_graph_compute_poll_for_work` loop also spins (bounded by `poll`) before it sleeps on the condvar; it is not changed here since the barrier was the dominant cost in these measurements.

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES — the investigation, the measurements and this patch were done with Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.1); the author reviewed and takes responsibility for the change.

title: CUDA: radix top-k for large row counts
body:
## Overview Replaces CUB's per-row DeviceTopKKernel with a grid-over-rows radix select, gated on GGML_CUDA_TOPK_RADIX_MIN_ROWS. Current implementation of top_k finding is sequential over rows (internal to a row, it is parallel). There is a for loop that goes over all the rows. The upstream top-k uses CPU processing over rows to loop over, but GPU processing internal to the row. This PR introduces radix select that is a single call at the op level that processes on the GPU completely and has a positive impact on the prefill perf. Also, the optimization applies to any model that calls ggml_top_k, with some conditionals on row and column count. Some examples that call ggml_top_k include deepseek32, deepseek4, minimax-m3. top_k calls are used after MOE router, with backend sampling, DFlash and Sparse-attention indexers.
Performance with various -lzm options on Qwen 3.8 Flash Next over DGX Spark

Six runs per arm over two rounds. Cold cache before every arm. Prompts from a 2.09M-word prose corpus so no two requests share n-grams — filler from a small vocabulary saturates the reachable n-gram set after one request and inflates the demand-paged arm. On/off order flipped between rounds. The on arm is I/O-bound, demand-paging a 26.8 GiB embedding table one fault at a time, so removing launches buys nothing there — hence its runs interleaving. An independent 2×2 at pp8192 agrees: 675.2 → 800.8 resident, 182.4 → 193.6 faulting. Decode is unchanged in every arm (~17.9–22.3 tok/s): ggml_top_k is not on this model's decode path at batch 1. **`--lazy-mode auto`** (resolves to OFF on this device, so the table is read resident) | run | prompt tok | radix on | radix off | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | 34,865 | 798.60 | 639.90 | | 2 | 34,661 | 804.00 | 644.60 | | 3 | 34,798 | 800.90 | 643.60 | | 4 | 34,812 | 805.40 | 658.80 | | 5 | 34,742 | 803.40 | 662.60 | | 6 | 34,733 | 804.00 | 662.40 | | | **mean** | **802.72 ± 2.50** | **651.98 ± 10.38** | | | **median** | 803.70 | 651.70 | **`--lazy-mode on-direct`** (from #28136 ) | run | prompt tok | radix on | radix off | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | 34,865 | 728.90 | 619.30 | | 2 | 34,661 | 737.00 | 622.10 | | 3 | 34,798 | 741.80 | 624.10 | | 4 | 34,812 | 733.90 | 616.40 | | 5 | 34,742 | 742.70 | 621.60 | | 6 | 34,733 | 748.10 | 625.70 | | | **mean** | **738.73 ± 6.87** | **621.53 ± 3.34** | | | **median** | 739.40 | 621.85 | **`--lazy-mode on`** (demand-paged mmap) | run | prompt tok | radix on | radix off | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | 34,865 | 214.40 | 196.80 | | 2 | 34,661 | 216.30 | 216.70 | | 3 | 34,798 | 247.40 | 233.50 | | 4 | 34,812 | 199.60 | 196.30 | | 5 | 34,742 | 227.60 | 218.00 | | 6 | 34,733 | 225.60 | 217.90 | | | **mean** | **221.82 ± 16.01** | **213.20 ± 14.31** | | | **median** | 220.95 | 217.30 | Summary: | `--lazy-mode` | radix on | radix off | effect of radix | |---|---|---|---| | `auto` (resident) | 802.72 ± 2.50 | 651.98 ± 10.38 | **+23.1%** | | `on-direct` | 738.73 ± 6.87 | 621.53 ± 3.34 | **+18.9%** | | `on` (demand-paged) | 221.82 ± 16.01 | 213.20 ± 14.31 | +4.0%, inside noise |

title: [DRAFT]: Formalizing scheduler and async backend behavior through tests
body:
## Overview

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->
This draft PR takes a first stab at formalizing the behavior of the scheduler and the async backends through test coverage.
There is lots to improve here, and I look forward to do so with your input. The main contribution is `test-backend-sched.cpp`. To create more complex test-cases, I also added a new operator `OP_SLEEP` (see below for details). 

I've implemented several classes of tests for this:

1. Test for formalizing behavior: Testing memcpys of user inputs and activations from and to every present backend, and also tests for specific patterns (e.g. Y-shaped graphs)
2. Tests reproducing current bugs and confirming proposed fixes (https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/26040). The failing test-cases here (using vulkan) are a feature; the PR by @0cc4m lets all current tests (as of August 17th) succeed. Also, https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/25319 fails, too (@JohannesGaessler).
3. Stress tests which test scheduling of simple (linked-list) and more complex (directed acyclic graph) schedules.

### New OP_SLEEP

* to create a reliable bug repro for https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/26040, I needed a way to consistently delay device processing. I landed on `OP_SLEEP` as opposed to some big MatMul for the following reasons:
  * `OP_SLEEP` was easy to implement in this scope (CPU, CUDA, VK)
  * sleep is not machine specific, so correlation between devices in CI and on local developer machines (=better GPUs) is easier
  * reproduction of errors is easier as sleep can be in-/decreased very granularly
  * Will be run run millions of times in CI going forward, so reduces resource waste a bit.
* If specific platforms do not support it, a proxy for it could still be a large enough MatMul / other expensive ops on the specific devices. Need input from the respective backend maintainers if this op can be implemented in their backend.

### TODO

* tests are currently very CPU/CUDA-centric, since these are the platforms I have easy access to, and to keep it simple. Will increase scope to vulkan and will integrate opportunistic testing. Whatever backend is present will be tested.
* Test improvements (pseudo-random small sleeps inside the stress tests to trip up scheduling)
* More tests for weird shapes (eg "X"-shaped) graphs

title: Performance tune for gemma4-26b-a4b flash attention shape.
body:
# sycl : fix missing gqa_ratio % 8 dispatch case in tile FA kernel for D=512

After noticing markedly different performance between qwen3-36b-a3b and gemma-4-26b-a4b, growing at long contexts, I directed Claude to compare the performance on long contexts, looking specifically at Gemma's global-attention layers (key_length = 512) vs Qwen's 256. Both models write an identical 20,480 bytes of KV per context token — Gemma across 5 full-attention layers of 30, Qwen across 10 of 40.

A roofline analysis looking specifically at `test-backend-ops perf -o FLASH_ATTN_EXT -b SYCL0 -p "nh=2,"` showed gemma4's speed around 16% of peak vs. qwen's 32% of peak on Intel Arc Pro B70.

This is Claude's description,

> `launch_fattn_tile_switch_ncols2()` (`ggml/src/ggml-sycl/fattn-tile.hpp`) picks the GQA broadcast width (`ncols2`) for the tile flash-attention kernel by testing `gqa_ratio` against descending divisors. The `DV == 256` branch tests `% 8 == 0` before `% 4 == 0`. The `DV == 512` branch does not — it goes straight from `% 16 == 0` to `% 4 == 0`.

The code patch is small enough to read directly rather than describing.

Note Gemma-4's global-attention layers use `gqa_ratio == 8` (head_count_kv=2, 16 query heads -- a multiple of 4 but not 16. Before this patch, `DV == 256` gets the full `ncols2=8` KV-tile reuse but `DV == 512` silently falls back to `ncols2=4`, halving KV-tile reuse per load for that shape. The `ncols2=8` config row and `launch_fattn_tile_switch_ncols1<..,8,..>` path already exist and are exercised by the `DV<=256` branch — they just aren't reachable when `DV==512`.

## Fix

Add the missing `% 8 == 0` check to the `DV == 512` branch, mirroring `DV <= 256`:

## Test case added

`make_test_cases_perf()` already has an `hsk=hsv=512, nh=1, nr23=[8,1]` case (`gqa_ratio=8`,
same dispatch bug), but nothing at `nh=2`, which is Gemma-4-26B-A4B's actual global-attention
shape (`head_count_kv=2`, 16 query heads). Added the `nh=2` counterpart next to it.

## Testing

Hardware: Intel Arc Pro B70 (32GB), driver 1.15.38646+7, oneAPI 2026.1 (icpx/icpx),
`GGML_SYCL_F16=ON`.

**Isolated op benchmark** (`test-backend-ops perf -o FLASH_ATTN_EXT`, Gemma-4 26B-A4B's real global-attention shape: `hsk=hsv=512, nh=2, nr23=[8,1]`, f16 KV), built at `a7b0709` (descendant of #21654 / #25205 / #26441, before this fix and before this file's next upstream touch):

```
before: kv=16384   756.34 GFLOPS   kv=65536   754.87 GFLOPS   kv=131072   766.72 GFLOPS
after:  kv=16384  1682.00 GFLOPS   kv=65536  1808.00 GFLOPS   kv=131072  1817.00 GFLOPS
```

2.2-2.4x per op. `hsk=256` at the same `nr23=[8,1]` measures ~1.78-1.85 TFLOPS at the same kv depths on this card — D=512 now lands in the same band instead of ~2.4x below it.
`fattn-tile.hpp` is untouched by any commit between `a7b0709` and current master
(`6a1a922d269908a29cbd4b49c27e6a8e7fd10fae`).

I prepared this PR against the current master with Claude's patch and the
new test case applied. The performance gain holds:

```
nh=1 (existing case): kv=49152  1.72-1.73 TFLOPS
nh=2 (added case):    kv=49152  1.77 TFLOPS
```

consistent with the `a7b0709` before/after above.

**Correctness**: `test-backend-ops test -o FLASH_ATTN_EXT -b SYCL0` — 4036/4037 pass, before and after, including the new `nh=2` case. Expected: `ncols2=4` vs `ncols2=8` are both correct tilings of the same computation, so this is a pure dispatch/perf fix, not a numerics change.

> [WARNING!]
>
> I noticed a pre-existing test failure `hsk=256, nh=2, nr23=[16,1], kv=1025, nb=64, permute=[0,2,1,3], type_K=type_V=q8_0`.
> It is unrelated to this PR. `GGML_SYCL_MKL_FA_DEBUG=1` shows it dispatches to `ONEDNN`, not `TILE`, and it fails identically with this patch reverted. Reproducible, (ERR ~1.2-1.3 across repeated runs).
>
> That needs to be fixed in a separate PR!
> Recent commits to llama.cpp have been working on SYCL backend ops (e.g. 4d9176092d005), and may be in the process of addressing that.

**End-to-end**: `llama-server`, same box, real model
(`unsloth/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf`, `-fa on`), decode tok/s by depth, synthetic filler prompt, greedy decode, isolated slot:

| depth | before | after | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| ~16 | 65.6 | 74.8 | +14% |
| 16,384 | 43.1 | 46.8 | +9% |
| 65,536 | 29.4 | 38.4 | +31% |
| 131,072 | 21.0 | 31.2 | +49% |

*Improvement grows with depth*, as expected since attention's share of per-token cost grows with kv while MoE FFN cost is flat.

## Requirements

- [X] I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- [X] AI usage disclosure:
Root cause found and patch written by Claude (Claude Code), from a manual read of the dispatch cascade in `fattn-tile.hpp` after isolating the regression with `test-backend-ops`. All benchmark numbers above were captured by the same tool runs cited. I reviewed this and wrote the PR.

title: jinja : fix use-after-free when {% filter %} is executed concurrently
body:
## Overview

`filter_statement::execute_impl` moves its `filter` child out of the AST node into a temporary `filter_expression` and moves it back afterwards:

```cpp
filter_expression filter_expr(std::move(parts), std::move(filter));
value out = filter_expr.execute(ctx);
this->filter = std::move(filter_expr.filter);
```

The compiled chat template is shared by all `llama-server` HTTP worker threads and rendered without a lock, so two overlapping requests that render the same `{% filter %}` node race on that `unique_ptr`: one thread frees the node while another still uses it. The visible symptoms are spurious `400 Invalid filter expression` responses under concurrent load, and eventually a crash of the whole server.

This PR applies the filter through a static helper that borrows the node (`const statement_ptr &`) instead of taking ownership, removes the sink constructor and `val` member that only existed for the move, and initialises `statement::pos`. Template output is unchanged.

## Additional information

To reproduce, start `llama-server --jinja` with any template that contains `{% filter %}` (the in-tree `models/templates/fireworks-ai-llama-3-firefunction-v2.jinja` is one) and let a handful of clients keep posting chat requests with a few hundred messages each, so that many `{% filter %}` executions overlap. The 400 errors appear immediately; an AddressSanitizer build dies within seconds, and a ThreadSanitizer build reports the race at `common/jinja/runtime.cpp:385` on the first overlap.

ASan report from the unpatched build at `c6824a9e4` (HTTP worker thread):

```
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: SEGV on unknown address 0x000d0000b341 (READ)
    #0 __dynamic_cast                                       libstdc++
    #1 jinja::filter_expression::execute_impl               common/jinja/runtime.cpp
    #3 jinja::filter_statement::execute_impl
    #5 jinja::for_statement::execute_impl
    #13 autoparser::autoparser::analyze_template
    #15 common_chat_templates_apply
    #16 oaicompat_chat_params_parse                         tools/server/server-common.cpp
    #25 httplib::ThreadPool::worker
```

## Requirements

title: spec : support DFlash for HunyuanOCR
body:
## Overview

Add DFlash speculative decoding support for HunyuanOCR.

## How to run

```bash
MODELS=./models/HunyuanOCR

# 1. base model + vision projector
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py "$MODELS" --outtype f16 --outfile hyocr-f16.gguf
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py "$MODELS" --outtype f16 --mmproj --outfile mmproj-hyocr-f16.gguf

# 2. DFlash draft
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py "$MODELS/dflash" \
    --target-model-dir "$MODELS" --outtype bf16 --outfile hyocr-dflash-bf16.gguf

# 3. serve
build/bin/llama-server \
    -m  hyocr-f16.gguf \
    --mmproj mmproj-hyocr-f16.gguf \
    -md hyocr-dflash-bf16.gguf \
    --spec-type draft-dflash --spec-draft-n-max 15 \
    --parallel 1 -fa on --jinja
```

## Results

Tested on an Apple M5 Pro (6 performance + 12 efficiency cores, 48 GB unified memory), macOS 26.4.1, Metal backend, Release build, over 26 document-image OCR requests:

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| draft acceptance | ~0.5 |
| mean accepted length | 8.6 |
| output | byte-identical to the non-speculative run |
| decode | 84.6 -> 167.1 t/s |
| prefill | 232 -> 192 t/s (the draft encodes the whole prompt) |

Decode is about 2x faster; prefill is about 17% slower because the draft encodes the entire prompt, so end-to-end is roughly break-even on short outputs and clearly faster on longer generations.

title: [ENH] server: tools: add "apptainer:" runtime support
body:
## Overview

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->

The PR adds "apptainer:" option support for `--tools-runtime`, in addition to "docker:" and "podman:". This is a continuation of #29024 after hardening apptainer instances.

## Additional information

<!-- You can provide more details and link related discussions here. Delete this section if not applicable -->

Podman is a more secure and open-source implementation of "docker". It allows a container inner "root" account which is converted back to normal uid/gid via setuid/setgid kernel support. The container can be modified, with e.g. local software installation.

An even more secure container solution is "apptainer", which is widely used in the HPC world. This type of container as a rather similar cli as podman/docker. The containers are by construction _immutable_, and the inner account when started is the launcher uid/gid. In here, only local 'pip'/'conda' can be installed (e.g. in `/tmp` or `/home` account), the rest of the system is fixed. In this implementation, no HOME is mounted, and only `/tmp is writable.

The behavior for the llama-server is exactly the same as the docker/podman solution already in place. The apptainer solution brings a high level security environment.

Here is a list of what has been changed/contributed:

| Area | Change in `server-tools.cpp` |
|---|---|
| `container_runtime_spec` | Adds the `apptainer` engine. `apptainer:<image>` spawns and is server-owned; `apptainer-instance:<name>` attaches. Adds `is_valid_image()` to reject option-like images. |
| `make_tools_io` | Unchanged logic, so the header path still refuses spawn forms and validates names. The error message now says "container or instance". |
| `tools_io_container::build_argv` | Apptainer branch runs `apptainer exec --pwd /tmp instance://<name> ...`. It adds no `-i`, which means `--ipc` in Apptainer, and `exec` forwards stdin anyway. |
| `server_tools_container_runtime` | Manages the instance lifecycle: `instance start --containall --writable-tmpfs <image> llama-tools-<random>`. It probes liveness with `exec ... true` and respawns a dead instance. The destructor runs `instance stop`. |
| Includes | Adds `<random>` for the instance name. |

**Security outcome**
- `--containall` hides the real `$HOME`, `/tmp` and environment. Risky `cat ~/.ssh/...` and `rm -rf ~` attacks no longer reach the host.
- `--writable-tmpfs` makes writes go to an in-memory overlay.
- A client header can only attach to an existing instance. It can never make the server pull or start an image.
- `--pwd /tmp` sets working directory to secured area in apptainer, removes the `chdir` warning, which would otherwise pollute the model's tool output.

**Tests (`test_tools_builtin.py`)**
- 9 header-rejection cases, which need no Apptainer binary.
- Attach via header, including persistent state across calls.
- A header cannot spawn an instance.
- Isolation with a canary file in `$HOME`, no warning, and cleanup on server exit.
- Respawn after an external `instance stop`.

## Requirements

title: vulkan: do not pin host memory past the host-visible heap budget
body:
## Overview

On amdgpu, offloading weights to host memory on a machine with limited RAM can kill the Vulkan context with no clear error message. The default offloadable RAM budget can be smaller than the weights, even though there are configurations that allow more RAM to be allocated for it, and there is no suggestion of what to change.

This PR makes the allocation fail while the device is still alive, so the existing unpinned fallback runs instead of the context being lost, and it names what to raise if you want to keep pinning.

host-visible (GTT) allocations are over-committed: `vkAllocateMemory` keeps succeeding after the pinned set no longer fits the heap, and the shortfall only surfaces at submit time as `radv/amdgpu: Not enough memory for command submission` -> `VK_ERROR_DEVICE_LOST`.

That happens after `ggml_vk_host_malloc` has already returned, so the existing fallback to an unpinned CPU buffer in `ggml_backend_vk_host_buffer_type_alloc_buffer` never runs, and neither does any fallback the caller has.

This PR queries `VK_EXT_memory_budget` before pinning and refuses while the device is still alive, so that fallback does its job. The reserve is gated on drivers that over-commit (`eMesaRadv`, `eAmdOpenSource`); drivers that fail the allocation are already handled and are left alone. `GGML_VK_HOST_PIN_RESERVE_MB` overrides it on any driver. On the drivers that need the reserve the warning also names the knob to raise (`amdgpu.gttsize`), so the "nothing tells you what to change" half of the problem is addressed too. Integrated GPUs are excluded by construction: their host-visible heaps are device-local, the loop matches no heap, and the helper reports "no budget information" rather than a budget of zero.

This is not VRAM exhaustion: on my machine the card has 24 GiB and peak VRAM use was ~8 GiB. The binding limit is the kernel's GTT budget, which amdgpu defaults to roughly half of system RAM and which no `VkPhysicalDeviceLimits` value exposes.

## Additional information

Hardware: Radeon RX 7900 XTX (RADV, Mesa 25.2.8, kernel 7.0.0-31), 30 GiB system RAM, default `mem_info_gtt_total` = 15591 MiB. Second GPU in the same box: RTX 5090.

Workload: stable-diffusion.cpp (same Vulkan backend) running Qwen-Image-2.1 Q8_0 at 1024x1024 with weights offloaded to host, which pins ~16.7 GiB if left alone. Instrumented `ggml_vk_host_malloc` to log the request, the `VK_EXT_memory_budget` figure and the running pinned total:

```
request= 969.04 MiB budget_avail=1898.39 MiB pinned_so_far=13677.22 MiB
request= 355.01 MiB budget_avail= 929.35 MiB pinned_so_far=14646.26 MiB
request= 483.09 MiB budget_avail= 573.95 MiB pinned_so_far=15001.27 MiB
request=   3.86 MiB budget_avail=  90.85 MiB pinned_so_far=15484.36 MiB
request=1152.00 MiB budget_avail=  86.98 MiB pinned_so_far=15488.22 MiB REFUSED
request=5184.00 MiB budget_avail=  86.98 MiB pinned_so_far=15488.22 MiB REFUSED
```

`VK_EXT_memory_budget` tracks the GTT heap accurately on RADV: `heapBudget - heapUsage` decreased in step with the pinned total and reached 86 MiB against a heap total of 15591 MiB.

Refusing only the allocations that exceed the remaining budget is not enough - by then the weights have taken 99.3% of the heap, and staging buffers and the submission itself come out of the same budget:

| build | pinned high-water | result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| master (pins everything) | not instrumented | device lost |
| budget check, no reserve | 15488 MiB | device lost |
| budget check, 1 GiB reserve | 14519 MiB | device lost |
| budget check, half the heap | - | completes, the rest left unpinned |

(the "no reserve" row already refuses the last two allocations, 1152 MiB and 5184 MiB, so its
high-water is lower than master's would be - master pins those too and still loses the device)

Why the reserve is gated. Same build and workload on the RTX 5090, toggling the reserve with
`GGML_VK_HOST_PIN_RESERVE_MB`, back to back in one run:

| RTX 5090 | wall | warning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| reserve disabled | 104.6 s | none |
| reserve on (half the heap) | 110.8 s | fires with 11695 MiB still free |

So on a driver that does not over-commit, the reserve costs 6% and refuses pinning while 11.4 GiB
of budget is free, for a failure mode that driver does not have.

Result with this PR as submitted (reserve gated):

| | master | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 7900 XTX (RADV) | device lost | completes, 75.2 s, one warning |
| RTX 5090 | not measured | completes, 102.0 s, no warning |

I did not run master on the 5090 for this workload, so I have no master baseline there; the 104.6 s
figure above is this branch with the reserve disabled, not master.

Both GPUs run through the Vulkan backend here - this build has no CUDA path - so the 5090 numbers
are not representative of that card and are only meant as an A/B against itself.

Weaknesses I am aware of:

- **No regression test.** Reproducing this needs a machine whose GTT budget is smaller than the model's pinned working set, which I do not know how to construct in CI. I am open to suggestions; if a test is required for this to be considered, say so and I will either find a way or close the PR.
- **The reserve fraction is empirical.** Half the heap is blunt, and the right number depends on how much staging the graph needs, which is not known at pin time. I preferred a bad default that degrades to "slower but alive" over the current "faster until the device is lost", but I have no principled way to pick it.
- Possibly the same root cause, both on amdgpu with a working set near the GTT budget: #27360, where the reporter's workaround is `--load-mode mmap`, i.e. not pinning.

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES. The patch and the first draft of this description were produced with an AI coding assistant (Claude Code) on my own hardware, from the debugging session in which I found the root cause. Every measurement quoted above was run on my machines. I have reviewed and edited this text manually, and I take responsibility for the change.
