## Overview

This PR adds support for the [SenseNova U1](https://github.com/OpenSenseNova/SenseNova-U1) text-generation branch in llama.cpp.

Supported use cases:

- Text-to-text generation
- Image-to-text generation
- Image-plus-text-to-text generation

The image path supports SenseNova U1’s dynamic-resolution preprocessing, 2D RoPE, patch embedding, spatial merge, and image-token injection.

The implementation is intentionally limited to U1’s understanding/text-generation branch. Image generation branch is not included.

## Additional information

Related to discussion #23529

Compile:
```bash
cmake -B build-u1-cuda \
  -DGGML_CUDA=ON \
  -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=90-real \
  -DLLAMA_BUILD_SERVER=ON \
```

```bash
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py \
```

title: [cuda]Make NCCL FP32/BF16 crossover threshold configurable
body:
**Incremental review:** [Files changed](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/27328/files) against `master`.

## Overview
This PR makes the NCCL FP32/BF16 crossover configurable through the `GGML_CUDA_NCCL_BF16_THRESHOLD` environment variable.

The threshold is specified in tensor elements and controls which communication dtype is used:

* tensors below the threshold use FP32;
* tensors at or above the threshold use BF16;
* invalid values automatically fall back to the existing default policy.

It also adds debug logging that reports the number of NCCL ranks, tensor element count, configured threshold, and selected communication dtype.

The default threshold remains unchanged, so this PR does not affect existing users unless the environment variable is explicitly set.
## Benchmark
Test configuration:

* Model: Qwen3.5-9B
* GPUs: 4× RTX 5060 Ti
* Workload: end-to-end prompt processing and generation
* Comparison: default policy, forced BF16, and forced FP32

| NCCL communication policy |      Prompt | Generation |
| ------------------------- | ----------: | ---------: |
| Default NCCL policy       | 107.2 tok/s | 20.5 tok/s |
| Forced BF16               | 104.4 tok/s | 20.1 tok/s |
| Forced FP32               | 111.9 tok/s | 21.4 tok/s |

Compared with forced BF16, forced FP32 improves:

* prompt processing by 7.18%;
* generation by 6.47%.

Compared with the current default policy, forced FP32 improves both prompt processing and generation by approximately 4.4%.

These results show that the optimal NCCL communication dtype depends on the workload and GPU topology. Exposing the crossover threshold allows users to tune this choice without changing the default behavior.

title: vulkan: fix wrong results when a mul_mat reads a slice of a larger cache
body:
## Overview

When GGML's Vulkan backend reads an attention cache view in place (the first n rows of a buffer that holds 5120), it assumed the heads were packed back to back while they are actually spaced by the full cache length, so every head but the first read the wrong data and the SheetSage2 decoder looped forever. The fix takes the real stride from the tensor instead of recomputing it from the visible row count, which also repairs the Qwen3 AR --no-fa path on Vulkan, and two new test-backend-ops cases lock it in.

## Additional information

Found while chasing https://github.com/ServeurpersoCom/yue2.cpp/issues/4, where the SheetSage2 decoder loops forever on Vulkan while it works on every other backend such as CPU and CUDA. This PR brings Vulkan in line with the others.

title: context : do not re-reserve the scheduler when toggling causal_attn
body:
## Overview

This PR removes the `sched_need_reserve = true` line from `llama_context::set_causal_attn()`, which previously marked the scheduler to do a full re-reserve on every change of the flag, and fixes the one architecture (`qwen4exp`) whose graph shape depended on the flag.

The re-reserve is unnecessary in this case because `causal_attn` only changes the values written to the KQ mask, not tensor shapes or any other buffer sizes. `qwen4exp` was the one exception that selected the per block/cell bias path based on the flag, so the causal and non-causal graphs differed in tensor shapes and ops. The second commit selects the block path independent of `causal_attn`, from the mask shape only and makes the non-causal case follow the reference rule: every visible block competes on score and only unpooled cells are always selected. The causal case works as before.


## Additional information
<!-- You can provide more details and link related discussions here. Delete this section if not applicable -->

For vision inputs, this flag is flipped twice around each non-causal image chunk for Gemma3, Gemma4, and DeepSeek-V4, resulting in two expensive `sched_reserve()` passes per image. This is especially slow for multi-image or video inputs.

The cost of a re-reserve scales with context and ubatch configurations, so larger settings pay more per image (see table below).

Note: `causal_attn` is a graph reuse key (`llm_graph_params` via `cparams`), so a new graph is built regardless of `sched_need_reserve`, so this doesn't change the graph rebuilding behaviour.

Speedup table: llama-server with gemma-4-26B-A4B Q4_0 + BF16 mmproj, 130-token images, cache_prompt=false, prompt_ms median of 3 (before -> after):

| images | config | H200 before -> after | RTX 4090 before -> after |
|-|-|-|-|
| 1 | `-c 8192 -ub 512` | 134 -> 105 ms (1.27×) | 201 -> 119 ms (1.69×) |
| 24 | `-c 8192 -ub 512` | 2278 -> 1562 ms (1.46×) | 3559 -> 1748 ms (2.04×) |
| 24 | `-c 32768 -ub 2048` | 5379 -> 1584 ms (3.40×) | 13377 -> 1759 ms (7.61×) |

Generated output remains identical before and after.

title: server : preserve context checkpoints across slot save/restore
body:
## Overview

Fix the full re-prefill after `slot save → restore` for SWA and hybrid/recurrent models (e.g. Qwen3.5 / Qwen3-Next).

When a slot is restored, the server rebuilds the token cache but not the context checkpoints (`slot->prompt.clear()` discards them, and they are not part of the save file). SWA and hybrid/recurrent models cannot rewind their state without a checkpoint, so the next divergent prompt triggers "forcing full prompt re-processing due to lack of cache data" even when it shares a long prefix with the saved state. Since a recurrent state cannot be rewound, checkpoints are not reconstructible after the fact, they have to travel with the save file.

This PR preserves the context checkpoints inside the slot save file:

- `save_slot_checkpoints()` appends a tagged payload (`SCKP` magic + version + count + per-checkpoint pos fields and state blobs) after the llama state payload
- `load_slot_checkpoints()` reads it back at the offset returned by `llama_state_seq_load_file` and reattaches the checkpoints to the slot
- Backward/forward compatible: old files restore exactly as before (no magic → silent skip), and new files load fine on older servers (they stop reading at the end of their own payload)
- Guards against corrupted files: count cap (1024), per-blob size cap, truncation → warning and clean abort (no partial state)
- `id_task` is not serialized and is reset to `-1` on load (task ids are not meaningful across save/restore)
- `n_written`/`n_read` include the appended checkpoint bytes, so the reported size matches the file on disk; no appendix is written when the slot holds no checkpoints, leaving those files byte-identical to the format without this feature

The change is confined to `tools/server/server-context.cpp` (+120 lines), using `std::ifstream`/`std::ofstream` with small read/write helpers. Total diff is 195 insertions and 2 deletions across the implementation and its test.

Independently reproduced and confirmed by 7 users across CUDA, Metal, Vulkan and an ollama integration, including a cross-machine CUDA → Metal restore. Details below.

## Additional information

Test included: `test_slot_restore_preserves_context_checkpoints` in `tools/server/tests/unit/test_slot_save.py`:

1. Send a long prompt (reference: a divergent re-prompt on the live slot rolls back to a checkpoint → partial reuse, `n_live` tokens processed)
2. `save` the slot
3. Overwrite the slot with an unrelated prompt
4. `restore` the slot
5. Send the same divergent re-prompt, the test asserts `prompt_n == n_live`

Without the fix, step 5 re-processes the full prompt. The fixture sets `cache_ram = 0` (the host prompt cache would otherwise mask the path under test) and `n_ubatch = 32` (so a prompt-processing checkpoint lands before the divergence point).

The new test passes locally against this branch after the rebase, and the same scenario fails on master (`assert 210 == 31`). The file now also carries the multimodal slot tests that came in with #26640; the full server suite is left to CI.

**Rebase note.** #26640 ("server : support slot save/restore with media inputs") reworked the same `SLOT_SAVE` / `SLOT_RESTORE` handlers: the save now writes a packed `server_tokens::serialize()` payload including media chunks instead of `get_text_tokens()`, and the restore does a two-pass `llama_state_seq_load_file` + `deserialize()` + `validate()`. This PR was rebased onto master and flattened to a single commit. The split is unchanged: the state payload belongs to master, the checkpoint appendix belongs to this PR, it is still appended after the payload, and the load offset is still the end of the payload returned by `llama_state_seq_load_file`.

Fixes #25913, same root cause reported there (checkpoints never persisted, cleared on restore).

Related: #22384 fixed the checkpoint lookup for recurrent models in a live slot; this PR addresses the save/restore path, which loses the checkpoints entirely.

User-reported results:

| Reporter | Date | Setup | Result |

title: webui: recognize audio/ogg MIME type in file uploads
body:
## Overview

Fixes #24164.

`getFileTypeCategory()` in `file-type.ts` only mapped `video/ogg` to a category. There was no `audio/ogg` entry in the `MimeTypeAudio` enum at all. When a browser reports an uploaded `.ogg` audio file as MIME type `audio/ogg` (which is standard), it doesn't match any case in the switch statement, so the file falls through to the plain-text handling path, fails the binary-content check, and gets silently skipped with an "appears to be binary" warning.

This adds `MimeTypeAudio.OGG = 'audio/ogg'` and routes it to `FileTypeCategory.AUDIO`, mirroring how `video/ogg` is already handled. Every other consumer of `MimeTypeAudio` (audio recording, the MCP `read_media` tool, playback format conversion) is intentionally narrower for an unrelated reason: those are constrained by the model's `input_audio` API, which only accepts MP3/WAV, so I left them untouched.

## Additional information

Verified via `svelte-check` (0 errors), `eslint`/`prettier` (clean), and a local test run through the project's vitest config covering the reported case, `video/ogg` staying unaffected, and existing audio types staying unaffected. No test file was added, per AGENTS.md guidance against adding tests for trivial changes.

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)

title: cuda: add F16 input to the FWHT
body:
## Overview

The CUDA FWHT accepts F32 input only. This makes the source type a template parameter, so
the kernel reads an F16 source directly instead of requiring a converted copy. The F32 path
is unchanged.

`supports_op` accepts an F16 `src1` against an F32 `src0` for the Hadamard hint. Every other
F16 `src1` against a non-F16 `src0` is still refused.

This is the CUDA counterpart to #27779 (CPU) and #29094 (Metal).

## Additional information

Tested on an H100 PCIe (compute capability 9.0, CUDA 12.8, `-DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=90`):

- `test-backend-ops -o MUL_MAT_HADAMARD` 15/15, including the six new F16 cases
- `test-backend-ops -o MUL_MAT` 1297/1297, run on the stacked tree that also carries #29100

The `supports_op` exception is narrow on purpose: the generic F32 src0 against F16 src1 path is
not implemented, so admitting a case the FWHT dispatch then declines would fall through to a
kernel that does not exist. #29094 has the Metal version of that same reasoning.

title: ci : update Level Zero SDK to v1.33.1 and enable the L0/oneDNN CMake flags in the SYCL job
body:
## Overview
Updates the SYCL CI environment to the current Level Zero SDK and enables the Level Zero API and oneDNN support that were installed but not enabled in the Ubuntu CI build. It also adds SYCL compiler flags used by the Linux `icpx` build.

## CI

Update `.github/workflows/build-sycl.yml`:

* Update Level Zero SDK v1.28.2 -> v1.33.1.

  * v1.33.x renamed the Debian packages to `libze1` / `libze-dev`.
  * Update the corresponding download URLs.
  * Update the Windows SDK zip as well.
* Enable `GGML_SYCL_SUPPORT_LEVEL_ZERO_API=ON` and `GGML_SYCL_DNN=ON` in the Ubuntu job.

  * The SDK was already installed, but these CMake options were not passed to the build, so Level Zero API and oneDNN support were disabled in CI.
* Add the following SYCL compile flag to the Linux `icpx` build:

  * `-fsycl-unnamed-lambda` - use stable kernel names to reduce JIT compilations.

## Windows note

`clang-cl` disables exceptions by default. Overriding `CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS` without `/EHsc` breaks non-SYCL targets with:

```text
cannot use 'throw' with exceptions disabled
```

Keep `/EHsc` when overriding the compiler flags. The existing Windows `.bat` script path is unaffected by this change.

## Additional information

See #29229

title: CUDA/HIP: matrix-core (MFMA) lightning indexer for CDNA2 (gfx90a)
body:
## Overview

This adds a ROCm matrix-core (MFMA) path for the DeepSeek-V3.2/V4 lightning indexer. The
current non-CUDA path runs the indexer on the scalar `lightning_indexer_kernel_vec`
kernel, which leaves the CDNA matrix cores idle; NVIDIA already has a tensor-core
(`wmma`) path 

The main motivation is DeepSeek-V4 long-context, where the lightning indexer scores every
KV token for top-k sparse-attention selection and its cost grows with context length.

## Performance

Tested with DeepSeek-V4 Flash GGUF (UD-IQ2_XXS, 84.6 GiB) on four MI250X (gfx90a) GCDs
using ROCm 7.2 (`-ngl 99 -fa on -sm layer -b 2048 -ub 512 -r 3`). Back-to-back A/B in the
same window; baseline is the existing `_vec` path (`GGML_INDEXER_NO_MFMA=1`).

title: [vulkan] Load F32 A matrix 2 at a time when its 2-aligned
body:
It turns out Intel doesn't particularly like loading F32s one at a time and we already have the _2aliagned load logic in mul_mat_vec, so here we use it.

While we do already check all the requirements to load elements 4 at a time across [B]F16 and F32, it turns out [B]F16 loading 4 at a time is sometimes slower on very specific shapes on Intel BMG. Loading 4 at a time is a bit faster on F32, but its not material and I assume might be slower on other platforms.

Note that we also need to validate `a_offset` is 2-aligned in `mul_mat_vec.comp`, which was missing in the original 2-way-load patch.

Some selected speedups from `test-backend-ops perf` on a B60 (obviously F32xF32 is pretty rare, but there are some steps that use it, so its nice to speed it up):

title: common: use physical core count for --threads -1 default
body:
Replace `std::thread::hardware_concurrency()` with `common_cpu_get_num_physical_cores()` for the `--threads -1` default value calculation.

`std::thread::hardware_concurrency()` returns logical CPU count, which includes hyper-threads, causing `--threads -1` to double-count on HT-enabled systems. `common_cpu_get_num_physical_cores()` already exists in `common/common.cpp` and returns the correct physical core count.

Fixes #19110

title: llama-vocab : add "sophia" pre-tokenizer type
body:
## Overview

Adds a new `sophia` pre-tokenizer type that performs no regex pre-splitting (`regex_exprs = {}`): the whole input is processed as a single byte-level BPE sequence, not even split on newlines.

This is needed to run GGUFs of [Sophia](https://huggingface.co/Arain119/sophia), a ~1B-parameter Chinese LM (KDA + MLA hybrid layers). Its weights map onto the existing `kimi-k3` graph at conversion time, so no model-side changes are needed - the vocab is the only missing piece for stock llama.cpp.

## Additional information

Why a new pre-type instead of an existing one:

Sophia's released `tokenizer.json` declares three `Split` pre-tokenizers, but they are serialized as `pattern.String` literals that never match (our tokenizer training script passed plain `str` patterns to `pre_tokenizers.Split` instead of wrapping them in `tokenizers.Regex`, which the library then serializes as literal `String` patterns). Combined with `ByteLevel(use_regex=false)`, the effective behavior of the shipped tokenizer is plain byte-level BPE over the entire input - which is also why the merges table contains newline-bearing pairs like `Ċ`+`Ċ`.

The model was pretrained with this tokenizer, so the behavior is baked into the weights; "fixing" the patterns would make token IDs diverge from what the model saw during training.

Closest existing alternatives don't fit:

- `deepseek-v3` splits the eval prompt set into 243 tokens where HF produces 151
- `superbpe` also avoids whitespace splitting but applies digit grouping, which this tokenizer never learned - only 1/10 digit-heavy test strings matched HF tokenization

Validation:

- Tokenizer parity vs HF `tokenizers`: 151/151 identical token IDs on the eval prompt set
- Teacher-forced logit parity vs PyTorch reference: 145/150 argmax agreement, mean |dlogprob| ~0.014 (divergent positions are near-ties)

Naming: happy to rename to something generic like `bytelevel-nosplit` if preferred, or close this and maintain it downstream if a model-specific pre-type isn't a good fit upstream.

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES - the patch was drafted by an AI coding agent (Devin) at my direction. I reviewed every line, built it, and ran the parity validation above myself.

title: common: add --no-mmap-prefetch to skip MADV_WILLNEED for large models
body:
## Problem

`ml.init_mappings(true, ...)` always prefetches model weights via `MADV_WILLNEED`. On macOS this is **blocking** and reads the entire model file into page cache. For models larger than roughly half of RAM (e.g. a 434 GB model on a 128 GB host), loading hangs for a long time and thrashes swap.

## Change

Add `llama_model_params.mmap_prefetch` (default `true` — no behavior change for existing users) plus a `--no-mmap-prefetch` CLI flag:

- `include/llama.h`: new `mmap_prefetch` bool (kept with the other booleans).
- `src/llama-model.cpp`: default `true` in `llama_model_default_params()`; `load_tensors` now passes `params.mmap_prefetch` to `init_mappings`.
- `common/common.h` / `common/arg.cpp` / `common/common.cpp`: `--no-mmap-prefetch` flag wired through `common_params`.

Small models keep the first-token latency win; large models can skip the multi-hour blocking prefetch.

title: llama-mmap: don't use MAP_POPULATE on Linux
body:
Unlike other hints, it's a blocking call that forces everything to load immediately.
Other platforms supposedly don't behave like this.
Originally added in f963b63afa and unchanged/unchallenged (no reason to use it found).

## Overview

This flag causes troubles on Linux specifically.
Just an example: may need to load a huge model while using mmap, for one reason or another. Any attempt to do it will start with pointless but very long step of reading all weights at startup (and subsequently paging them out by OS). There seems to be no proper way to disable this behaviour gracefully, every option is not directly related to this.

## Additional information

According to what I found, PrefetchVirtualMemory on Windows is a non-blocking hint too, just like madvise calls on POSIX path. MAP_POPULATE blocks each mmap call which can even be less efficient than async loading. It can also cause memory pressure detection mechanism to crash user session when model size is big enough (but not necessarily exceeding RAM).

title: cuda: FWHT kernels for block widths above 512
body:
## Overview

The CUDA FWHT covers block widths 64 to 512. It runs one row per warp and keeps `N/32`
values per lane, so wider blocks need more registers per lane than that layout allows.

`fwht_cuda_block` runs one row per thread block with 256 threads, so each thread keeps
`N/256` values instead. Stages below the warp width still shuffle, those up to the block
width go through shared memory, and the rest stay in registers. The butterfly and sign
convention match the existing kernel.

Widths 64 to 512 keep the warp kernel and are untouched. 1024 through 8192 use the new
one, for both F32 and F16 sources.

This is the CUDA counterpart to #29095 (Metal). Stacked on #29096; the last commit is the
one to review here.

## Additional information

Tested on an H100 PCIe (compute capability 9.0, CUDA 12.8, `-DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=90`):

- `test-backend-ops -o MUL_MAT_HADAMARD` 25/25, including the new 1024/2048/4096/8192 cases
  in F32 and F16, and the 16384 case that falls back
- `test-backend-ops -o MUL_MAT` 1297/1297, no regressions

A passing suite does not by itself show the new kernel ran, since a Hadamard-hinted matmul that
falls back to the generic path computes the same values. To confirm the wide kernel is actually
selected I temporarily made `fwht_cuda_block` scale its output by 2 and re-ran, which gave
15/25 with exactly ten failures:

- the ten wide cases, 1024/2048/4096/8192 and 1024 with seven rows, in both F32 and F16, all failed
- all fourteen cases at 512 and below passed, which is the warp kernel that change does not touch
- 16384 also passed, confirming widths outside the supported list still take the generic path

The change was reverted and the binary rebuilt before the numbers above were taken.

8192 allocates 32 KB of shared memory per block, within the 48 KB default limit. If that is too
aggressive for older parts I am happy to cap the width list lower.

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES. Claude Code was used to write and test this change, following the
  structure of the existing warp kernel and the Metal version, and to format this description to
  the PR template. I reviewed every line and take full responsibility for the changes.

title: metal: FWHT kernels for block widths above 512
body:
## Overview

The Metal FWHT covers block widths 64 to 512. It runs one row per simdgroup and keeps
`N/32` values per lane, so wider blocks need more registers per lane than that layout
allows.

`kernel_fwht_tg` runs one row per threadgroup with 256 threads, so each thread keeps
`N/256` values instead. Butterflies below the simdgroup width still shuffle, those up to
the threadgroup width go through threadgroup memory, and the rest stay in registers. The
butterfly and sign convention match the existing kernel.

Widths 64 to 512 keep the simdgroup kernel and are untouched. 1024 through 8192 use the
new one, for both F32 and F16 sources.

## Additional information

Stacked on #29094, which adds the F16 source type. The last commit is the one to review here.

8192 allocates 32 KB of threadgroup memory, which is the limit on the devices I can test.
`ggml_metal_fwht_supported_size` stops there for that reason, and anything wider keeps the
existing behaviour of falling back to the generic matmul path.

Tested on an M5 Pro with `test-backend-ops`:
- `MUL_MAT_HADAMARD` 26/26, including the new 1024/2048/4096/8192 cases in F32 and F16
- `MUL_MAT` 1265/1265, no regressions

The previous "too big" test case moved from 1024 to 16384, since 1024 is now covered.

title: speculative : clamp draft context to n_ctx_train for unified KV
body:
Fixes #29148

## Overview
When using `--spec-type draft-mtp` with `--kv-unified`, the target context is scaled by the number of server slots (`n_seq_max * n_ctx_train`).

In `common_speculative_init_result`, the draft context was taking `cparams.n_ctx = llama_n_ctx(ctx_tgt);`, inheriting that entire multi-slot pool (e.g. 1M tokens instead of 262k for Qwen with `-np 4`). On Vulkan/CUDA, trying to allocate that extra 1M-token KV cache runs out of VRAM and fails to create the draft context.

- Clamped draft context to `std::min(llama_n_ctx_seq(ctx_tgt), n_ctx_train_tgt)`.
- Added the same clamp for external draft models against `n_ctx_train_dft`.
- Keeps existing behavior if `n_ctx_train == 0` or if the user explicitly set a smaller `-c`.

Tested with a synthetic MTP model and verified the draft context now allocates within trained limits.

title: test-save-load-state : compare logits with NMSE and feed expected tokens
body:
## Overview
`test-save-load-state` previously required exact token sequences to match between the baseline and restored contexts. This is too strict because small numerical differences in restored state can change a sampled token even when the underlying logits are effectively identical.

This PR changes tests 3, 4, and 5 to:
- Store the raw logits for every baseline generated token.
- Compare regenerated raw logits against the baseline using NMSE.
- Fail only if NMSE exceeds `1e-5`.
- Feed the expected baseline token back into the context when the sampled token differs, so the remaining logits stay aligned.

title: vulkan: add F16 input to the FWHT
body:
## Overview

The Vulkan FWHT accepts F32 input only. This adds an F16 source variant of the shader, for
both the subgroup and the shared-memory paths, so the kernel reads an F16 source directly
instead of requiring a converted copy.

The F16 shader needs shader-float16, so those pipelines are only created when the device
reports it. A null pipeline makes `ggml_vk_can_use_fwht` fall back, which is the same path an
unsupported width already takes. `supports_op` needed no change, since it already admits an
F32 src0 against an F16 src1.

This is the Vulkan counterpart to #27779 (CPU), #29094 (Metal) and #29096 (CUDA).

## Additional information

Tested on Apple M5 Pro through MoltenVK (`uma: 1 | fp16: 1 | warp size: 32 | shared memory: 32768`):

- `test-backend-ops -o MUL_MAT_HADAMARD -b Vulkan0` 15/15, including the six new F16 cases
- `test-backend-ops -o MUL_MAT -b Vulkan0` 1128/1128, no regressions

I verified the F16 cases actually reach the new kernel rather than falling back, by instrumenting
`ggml_vk_can_use_fwht` to print the selected pipeline: `pipeline_fwht_f16[idx]` is non-null and
selected for every F16 case. That instrumentation is not part of this PR.

Worth noting for anyone testing this: `GGML_VK_PERF_LOGGER=1` cannot confirm it. Its labels come
from `get_node_fusion_name`, which builds the string from `ggml_op_name(node->op)` and appends
`_VEC` when `n <= mul_mat_vec_max_cols`. It describes the graph node, not the pipeline that ran,
so a Hadamard-hinted MUL_MAT logs as `MUL_MAT_VEC` whether or not the FWHT kernel executed.

MoltenVK is a translation layer, so this is not equivalent to a native driver. All four shader
variants also compile standalone under `glslc --target-env=vulkan1.3`. A run on native Intel, AMD
or NVIDIA would be worth having before this is relied on, and I would welcome one.

Separately, and not introduced by this PR: on Intel Windows drivers inside the
`[32.0.101.8509, 32.0.101.8860)` range gated at ggml-vulkan.cpp:3315, no FWHT pipeline is created
at all, so `MUL_MAT_HADAMARD` passes there via the generic fallback without ever executing the
kernel. That applies to the existing F32 path too. It means green CI on such a device is weaker
evidence than it appears.

title: ggml-sycl: remove dpct (SYCLomatic) emulation layer, switch to out-of-order queues with native sycl::event dependencies
body:
## Summary

Removes the dpct (SYCLomatic) emulation layer from the SYCL backend and replaces it with native SYCL 2020 primitives. The dpct layer left over from the original CUDA→SYCL conversion — `dpct::dev_mgr` (a CUDA-style thread→device map with mutex-protected `device_ext` wrappers) and in-order queues — causes stalls and deadlocks with Level Zero V2 (Immediate Command List) runtimes and adds host-side latency on every queue access.

### What changed

**De-dpct / heritage cleanup**
- Delete `dpct/helper.hpp` (3782 lines) and replace its primitives with `ggml_sycl::` implementations in the new `sycl_core.hpp`:
  - `device_registry` — plain `sycl::device::get_devices()` enumeration (honors `ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR`, same as dpct did) + lazily created **out-of-order** `sycl::queue` per device. No thread→device map, no mutex-wrapped `device_ext`, no in-order queues.
  - Native `sycl::event` dependency control: every command submitted on a queue depends on the previous command's event (`ordered_submit`, `ordered_parallel_for`, `ordered_memcpy`, `ordered_memset`, `ordered_barrier`, `ordered_single_task`), reproducing in-order semantics without the `in_order` queue property, op-boundary barriers, or host synchronization. The runtime releases each event automatically once its dependents complete.
  - Subgroup shuffle via `sycl::select_from_group` (exact port of `dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor`), `dp4a`, `device_info` via `sycl::get_info`, oneMKL gemm wrappers, `memcpy_async`, error codes, launch dims.
- Adapt the backend interface: init, buffer types, event record/wait (now captures the stream's last event directly instead of submitting a barrier), split-tensor mul_mat synchronization, and `ggml_sycl_set_main_device` (thread-local current device kept only for fast paths).

**Performance tuning** (measured on Arc B570, oneAPI 2026.1, Qwen3.8-9B Q4_K_M, -ngl 99)
- Gate off the Q4_K GLU-fused MMVQ kernel: it is occupancy-limited by register pressure (2 weight sets + shared activations in flight; VTune occupancy 32.7%) and two unfused MMVQ kernels are ~10% faster (54.8 vs 50.0 t/s tg128). The kernel code is kept and the gate is a single `return false;` for easy re-enabling after register-pressure work.
- GLU fused MMVQ launcher: 256 → 128 threads per work group (+12% when fusion is used) — a 256-thread WG with SIMD16 fills all 8 XVE thread slots of one XVE, but only ~3 slots are actually resident with the fused kernel's register pressure.
- ESIMD DMMV: work-group size 4 → 8 (+0.5%).
- Add the missing `template-instances/` (56 generated FA kernel instances referenced by `file(GLOB ...)` in CMakeLists.txt but not committed).

**CI (`.github/workflows/build-sycl.yml`)**
- Update Level Zero SDK v1.28.2 → v1.33.1 (v1.33.x renamed the Debian packages to `libze1`/`libze-dev` — download URLs updated accordingly; Windows SDK zip updated).
- Enable `GGML_SYCL_SUPPORT_LEVEL_ZERO_API=ON` and `GGML_SYCL_DNN=ON` in the Ubuntu job (the SDK was installed but the CMake flags were never passed, so Level Zero and oneDNN support were silently disabled in CI builds).
- Add SYCL compile flags: `-fsycl-unnamed-lambda` (stable kernel names → fewer JIT compiles), `-fsycl-id-queries-fit-int`, `-fsycl-fp-contract=fast` (Linux icpx; unknown/ignored by the Windows clang-cl driver, so the Windows job is unaffected).

### Note for Windows users

`-fsycl-id-queries-fit-int` and `-fsycl-fp-contract=fast` are Linux (icpx GNU-driver) flags — the Windows clang-cl driver ignores them with a warning. Also, clang-cl disables exceptions by default: overriding `CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS` without `/EHsc` breaks non-SYCL targets ("cannot use 'throw' with exceptions disabled") — keep `/EHsc` when overriding flags (the Windows bat script path is unaffected by this PR).

## Verification

- **Build**: full build (493 targets) with oneAPI 2026.1 + `icx` on Windows, `GGML_SYCL_SUPPORT_LEVEL_ZERO_API=ON`, `GGML_SYCL_DNN=ON`, `GGML_SYCL_F16=ON` — success.
- **Correctness**: `test-backend-ops -b SYCL0` → **17,977/17,996 tests passed**. The 19 remaining failures (CONV_2D cwhn=1 kernels ×16, ROLL, FLASH_ATTN_EXT hsk=256/kv=1025, FA vec-slice test) fail identically on the pre-refactor baseline — they are pre-existing issues in this backend, not caused by this change.
- **Performance** (llama-bench, Qwen3.8-9B Q4_K_M, -ngl 99, vs the official `b10899` release build on the same machine):
  - `pp512`: **1309–1464 t/s vs 431 t/s → 3.0–3.4x**
  - `tg128`: **44.5–49.7 t/s vs 29.6 t/s → 1.5–1.7x** (and 54.8 t/s with the GLU fusion gated off)
  - No deadlocks or hangs under the Level-Zero V2 runtime (`Intel(R) oneAPI Unified Runtime over Level-Zero V2`).
- **GPU hotspots (VTune)**: out-of-order queues + native event chains work correctly with L0 V2; the remaining hot kernels are the Q6_K/Q4_K ESIMD DMMV and the (now gated-off) GLU fused MMVQ.

title: common : strip matching quotes from INI preset values
body:
## Overview

Router `--models-preset` kept surrounding `"` / `'` on INI values. A line like

    model = "D:\llama-cpp\models\foo.gguf"

was passed through as `--model` with the quote characters still in the path, so `gguf_init_from_file` failed with Invalid argument. Standalone `-m "D:\..."` works because the shell strips the quotes.

This drops one matching outer `"` or `'` after INI capture. Backslashes are left as-is so Windows paths stay intact. JSON object values such as `chat-template-kwargs = {"reasoning_effort": "high"}` are unchanged because they do not start and end with the same quote.

Fixes #29225

## Additional information

The PEG `value` rule is `(!eol-start .)*`, so the quotes are captured as part of the text. Unquoted paths are unchanged. Quoted paths that contain spaces parse correctly after the outer quotes are removed.

Regression coverage is in `tests/test-arg-parser.cpp`: quoted Windows path, quoted POSIX path with spaces, unquoted POSIX path, single-quoted POSIX path, and JSON kwargs.

## Requirements

title: CUDA: fix sm_70 tile compilation error
body:
## Overview

Fixes #29222.

The 5-argument `load_ldmatrix` added in 1884824fd only defined `tile<16, 8>`, so the Volta `tile<8, 4>` used by sm_70 had no matching overload and `fattn.cu` failed to compile.

This PR generalizes the 5-argument `load_ldmatrix` tile shape from `<16, 8>` to `<I, J>`. The non-swizzle branch forwards to the 3-argument loader, so any tile shape works. The swizzle branch is restricted to `<16, 8>` with newly added `static_assert(I == 16)` / `static_assert(J == 8)`.

This follows the existing pattern of `load_ldmatrix_trans` in the same file, which is already shape-generic plus `static_assert(I == 16)`.

Only sm70 was affected; other architectures were checked. CI does not build sm70, so this was not caught.

Local compile and test passed.

title: ggml-cuda : convert contiguous tensors four elements at a time
ggml-cuda: fallback to F32 on device without BF16 hardware acceleration
body:
## Overview

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->

Older AMD GPUs (pre-CDNA / pre-RDNA3) do not have native BF16 matrix acceleration, and rocBLAS has no tuned BF16 kernel for them. On these older card a BF16 GEMM can land on a 64x32x8 stub tile.

This PR add a fallback from BF16 to F32 on pre-CDNA / pre-RDNA3 AMD GPUs because rocBLAS does not provide a properly tuned BF16 GEMM path there.

Applies to UD/*_XL quants that keep BF16 tensors.

```
BF16 path:
    convert activations F32 -> BF16: O(K * N)
    BF16 x BF16 GEMM with F32 accumulation

F32 fallback:
    convert weights BF16 -> F32: O(M * K)
    F32 x F32 GEMM
```

During testing on my gfx906 this gives large prefill improvements for sufficiently large GEMMs, but benchmarking showed that doing the conversion unconditionally introduces a significant regression for small `N`.

After some tests on multiple models (differents count of BF16 and different GEMM shapes `(M,N,K)`) I added small check to keeps BF16 on AMD when `N <= 32` and switches to F32 when `N > 32`.

```cpp
        if (GGML_CUDA_CC_IS_AMD(ggml_cuda_info().devices[ctx.device].cc) && src1->ne[1] > 32) {
            compute_type = GGML_TYPE_F32;
        }
```

`src1->ne[1] > 32` corresponds to the GEMM N dimension.

I've only made the change for AMD. Nvidia GPU before Ampere does not have native BF16 matrix acceleration eather but I do not own a Nvidia card to test this. Feel free to complete/remove the todo if revelant.

## Additional information

<!-- You can provide more details and link related discussions here. Delete this section if not applicable -->

 Why N > 32 ?

Whitout the thresold, on small N <=32 :
- Qwen3-14B: F32 was ~10.5% slower
- Qwen3-4B:  F32 was ~7% slower
- Llama 3.1 8B: F32 was ~3% slower
- Gemma 3 12B: F32 was ~8% slower

N=32 Seems to be the crossover. The generic HIP fallback library contains: `Cijk_Ailk_Bjlk_BSS_BH_MT64x32x8_...`
which seems to always fallback to the `64x32x8` macro-tile and several other fallback solutions also use a free-dimension tile of 32. This does not necessarily mean that the 64x32x8 macro-tile alone causes the crossover: rocBLAS can select different solutions depending on the complete (M, N, K) shape. However, the exact 32 -> 33 transition was observed across models with very different shapes, which makes the N > 32 threshold a good fit.

Tested models:
- Qwen3-4B
- Qwen3-8B
- Qwen3-14B
- Llama 3.1 8B
- Gemma 3 12B
- Gemma 4 E4B

title: ggml: allow prefetching tensor overrides
body: ## Overview This PR adds support to prefetch tensor overrides for each layer, overlapping with the compute for the current layer. Only the CUDA implementation is provided, guarded by the `--prefetch-weights` flag. At this stage I would consider this a PoC, so keeping as draft for now for comments and further tests. > Note that `--no-mmap` is necessary for this work, otherwise the operations are implicitly serialized due to the weights not being pinned. # Performance Analysis ## Dense Models For dense models, the optimization is relatively straightforward. Let's call $C_{n}$ the time taken for computing the $n^{th}$ layer on the GPU, and $T_{n+1}$ the time to transfer layer $n^{th}+1$ weights from the CPU to the GPU. If you choose to override weights on the CPU, then this overlaps $T_{n+1}$ with $C_{n}$, whereas currently everything happens sequentially. So if $C_{n} > T_{n+1}$ we can "hide" the transfer latency and have it behave like a GPU. Although when $C_{n} >> T_{n+1}$, $C_{n}$ dominates so this is less useful. On the other hand, decreasing $T_{n+1}$ is only possible using newer hardware like PCIe Gen5 or using lower bpw. There are two natural dimensions where we can increase $C_{n}$ without increasing $T_{n+1}$, those are `ubatch` size and the kv-cache `depth`. Here is a graph using a relatively recent model, since this is a linear attention model, the compute doesn't go up as fast a quadratic attention model with increasing depth. We override `ffn_(gate|up|down).*` to the CPU, which are the bulk of the weights in each layer. We can see it benefits at all batch sizes, but the gap is lesser at higher batch sizes (since $C_{n}$ starts to dominate) `llama-bench -m /opt/models/Qwen3.5-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf -fa 1 -p 2048 -ub 512,1024,2048 -d 0,10000,20000,30000,40000,50000 -n 0 -ot "ffn_(gate|up|down).*=CPU" -pw 0,1 --mmap 0` ## MoE models For MoE models, the situation is different because of selective copying of experts (added in #15346). This is a massive improvement for smaller ubatch sizes, naturally prefetching cannot do this as it does not know which experts will be selected in the next layer. The situation is worse for larger MoE models with more experts and larger inner dims, so likely this will be slower for large MoE models unless they are deep (more layers) and not wide (larger expert dims). The equation for prefetching to be beneficial becomes $C_{n} + T_{c}' > T_{c+1}$, where $T_{c}'$ is the time to transfer the selected experts for the $n^{th}$ layer. The same stuff applies, if we scale $C_{n}$ it becomes more beneficial, but we can also scale $T_{c}'$ by increasing the ubatch size, hence increasing expected number of used experts in a `ubatch`. In the graph below we see comparable performance at `ubatch`=512, but much better at 1024,2048. Since 50k context fully fits on this GPU, I also the added the theoretical maximum of fully offloading to the GPU `llama-bench -m /opt/models/gpt_oss-20b-mxfp4.gguf -fa 1 -p 2048 -ub 512,1024,2048 -d 0,10000,20000,30000,40000,50000 -n 0 -ncmoe 999 -pw 0,1 --mmap 0`. ## Requirements - I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md) - AI usage disclosure: YES, I used AI to write parts of the code, and I used it for debugging the ggml-backend code while struggling with the graph allocator. I have reviewed and tested it myself.

title: Windows: raise stdio limit for loading many GGUF shards
body:
## Overview

This PR raises the maximum number of stdio handles on Windows at startup so llama.cpp can load models split across many `.gguf` shards without hitting the default Windows/MSVC file handle limit.

On Linux, this is commonly handled externally with `ulimit`, but Windows does not provide the same mechanism for end users. Calling `_setmaxstdio()` in the binary gives Windows builds comparable behavior and avoids shard-loading failures for heavily sharded models.

## Additional information

The new limit is set conservatively to `2048`, which is below MSVC’s documented hard cap of `8192`. If `_setmaxstdio()` fails, the code logs the failure and continues with the default runtime limit.

I have been using this change in a downstream fork for more than 8 months without issues.

title: server: add router device memory margin parameter for dynamic unloading
body:
## Overview

I have a server running which serves small embedding models and large text models. Currently there's no way to allow multiple small models to coexist in memory, but to unload them when a large model needs space. This PR solves that by adding a `--models-memory-margin` parameter which works similarly to the autofit feature memory margin. The router keeps track of memory requirements per model and uses it to unload models in the same order as previously defined for the max number of models, once that margin is exceeded on any device.

I've been running this on my server and it solves the issue I had.

# Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES, Qwen3.5 122B and Claude were used for assistance.

title: ggml-cpu : add Q8_0 IME1 matrix kernel for SpacemiT X60
body:
## Overview

I have a Milk-V Jupiter board and wanted Q8_0 to run properly on the SpacemiT X60. The X60 already
had IME acceleration, but only for Q4_0/Q4_1/Q4_K. Q8_0 had no IME1 kernel at all, and because the
SpacemiT build sets `GGML_CPU_REPACK=OFF`, there was no repack path compiled in either — so Q8_0
had no accelerated path whatsoever and ran at about a tenth of Q4_0's prefill speed on the same
board. This PR adds the missing Q8_0 IME1 kernel.

This replaces #28025, which I closed. That version was M1-only and reached 39.97 t/s prefill;
this one adds the 4-row path, which roughly doubles it again.

## Additional information

Changes:

- `make_block_q8_0x16` and the repack entry in `repack.cpp`: interleave Q8_0 weights into the
  16-column layout the IME1 `vmadot` sequence expects.
- `ime1::gemm_kernel_i8i8` in `ime1_kernels.cpp`: the int8 x int8 IME1 kernel, with both a single-row
  and a 4-row A path. The 4-row path loads each B panel once and reuses it across 4 rows of A, which
  is where most of the gain over the M1-only version comes from.
- `quantize_a_4row_i8`: the 4-row activation quantization the M4 path needs. In #28025 this was
  `nullptr` and `gemm_m >= 4` was forced back through the single-row path.
- wiring in `forward_mul_mat` and the repack factory for `block_q8_0`.
- docs: mark Q8_0 as supported on X60.

## Testing

Milk-V Jupiter (SpacemiT X60, 8 cores / 4 preferred, RVV1.0, VLEN=256), Bianbu 2.1.1, gcc 14.2.
Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, `llama-bench`, `-t 4` under `taskset -c 0-3`, 5 repetitions, board otherwise
idle.

Correctness: I compared the kernel against a quant-exact reference (dequantizing the same blocks and
doing the multiply in integer arithmetic, rather than against a float reference) for K = 32 up to
4096. Max relative error is ~1e-6, which is the expected float accumulation difference. I also
checked that generation stays coherent across several prompts.

Note that `test-backend-ops` does not exercise this kernel on a CPU-only build: it skips the CPU
backend and reports OK, so it cannot be used to validate this change.

Performance, pp128 prefill, before and after this change on the same build settings (both with IME1
enabled, so the only variable is the kernel):

| model             | before    | after     | speedup |
| ----------------- | --------: | --------: | ------: |
| Qwen2.5-0.5B Q8_0 | 10.70 t/s | 95.27 t/s |    8.9x |

The commit message quotes another run (Q8_0 93.87 t/s, Q4_0 107.51 t/s); the difference is
run-to-run variation.

For reference, Q4_0 on the same board measures 107.81 t/s with this change applied, against 106.40 t/s
before it, i.e. unchanged within run-to-run variation, which is what I would expect since this PR
does not touch that path.

I am only claiming prefill here. Token generation does improve, but Q4_0 token generation moved by
about 1.19x between the two builds despite that path being untouched, so I do not trust the
token-generation numbers enough to quote them as a result of this change.

## Requirements

title: CUDA: batch-invariant flash-attn for narrow widths on SM120
body:
### Problem

The flash-attention dispatch picks the narrowest template instance that fits `Q->ne[1]`. Speculative decoding varies `ne[1]` from step to step — 1 for the reference decode, 3–4 for the verification pass at the default `--spec-draft-n-max 3` — so one logical computation is served by two instances that differ in tile geometry, and therefore in KV loop and combine order. They cannot agree bitwise.

Speculative decoding is lossless under greedy sampling by construction, since the target model ratifies every drafted token. On SM120 today it is not: enabling it changes the generated text.

### Reproduction

`test_flash_attn_ext_batch_invariance` (added here) compares one batched pass against per-token serial passes with `memcmp` and `max_err() = 0`, over `n_kv {2048, 7168, 16384}` × `n_tokens {1, 2, 3, 4}`.

On an RTX 5080 Laptop, current master:

```
FLASH_ATTN_EXT_BATCH_INVARIANCE(n_tokens=3,n_kv=2048)    FAIL
FLASH_ATTN_EXT_BATCH_INVARIANCE(n_tokens=4,n_kv=2048)    FAIL
FLASH_ATTN_EXT_BATCH_INVARIANCE(n_tokens=3,n_kv=7168)    FAIL
FLASH_ATTN_EXT_BATCH_INVARIANCE(n_tokens=4,n_kv=7168)    FAIL
FLASH_ATTN_EXT_BATCH_INVARIANCE(n_tokens=3,n_kv=16384)   FAIL
FLASH_ATTN_EXT_BATCH_INVARIANCE(n_tokens=4,n_kv=16384)   FAIL
6/12 tests passed
```

`n_tokens` 1 and 2 pass; the failures are exactly the widths a 3-token draft produces.

End to end, Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q3_K_XL, `--temp 0 --seed 1 -fa on`, 640 tokens, same prompt:

| run | vs. non-speculative reference |
|---|---|
| `--spec-type ngram-mod`, master | **diverges** — different text from the first paragraph on |
| `--spec-type ngram-mod`, this PR | **byte identical** |

A low-entropy prompt (verbatim code edit) produced identical output either way, so whether it is user-visible depends on how close the top-2 logits are. The determinism property is broken regardless.

### Fix

On Blackwell, route widths 3 and 4 to the 4-wide vector tile, which widths 1 and 2 already reduce to. That leaves a single instance across the whole 1..4 range. Columns past `ne[1]` are masked and `ntiles_x` stays 1 over that range, so launch geometry is unchanged. `LLAMA_SM120_FA_INVARIANT=0` restores the stock dispatch.

With the change: `12/12 tests passed`.

### Cost

`test-backend-ops perf`, same card, hs 256 / 24 q-heads / 4 kv-heads / kv 7168 / q8_0 KV. Medians of interleaved runs, first round discarded. Widths 1, 2, 5 and 8 are controls — the change must not touch them:

| nb | master | this PR | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 87.44 µs | 87.32 | −0.1% |
| 2 | 132.52 | 132.62 | +0.1% |
| **3** | 159.56 | 185.81 | **+16.5%** |
| **4** | 162.04 | 187.15 | **+15.5%** |
| 5 | 184.16 | 182.83 | −0.7% |
| 8 | 186.38 | 186.16 | −0.1% |

The cost is confined to the affected widths, and it is not anomalous: it brings nb=3/4 to ~186 µs, which is what nb=5 and nb=8 already cost. The 4-wide tile does 4-wide-tile work.

An alternative that pins one MMA instance across widths 1..4 instead was measured and rejected — it is free at widths 3–4 (+0.4%) but costs **+84.5% at nb=1** and +21.2% at nb=2, i.e. it taxes ordinary single-token decode.

### Testing

- `test-backend-ops test -b CUDA0`: **14607/14607 passed, 2/2 backends**, no failures.
- Compiles clean for `CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=75;86;120`, and runtime behaviour is identical to a 120-only build.
- Hardware: RTX 5080 Laptop (SM120) only. The change is gated to Blackwell and leaves every other architecture on the existing dispatch — I cannot test whether other architectures have the same property.

title: CUDA : fix divergent FlashAttention barrier
body:
## Overview
Incorrect use of `__syncthreads()`  created divergent barriers in the FlashAttention code. It produced 1024 synchronization errors reported by NVIDIA Compute Sanitizer:
`compute-sanitizer --tool synccheck`. 
The issue is:
```
.... threads in the same block  ... 
if (thread_type_a) {
    .....
    __syncthreads(); // creates barrier A
} else {
   __syncthreads();  // creates barrier B
}
```
So the threads in the same block are running towards different barriers based on which branch they take.  
This can be fixed by:
```
.... threads in the same block ... 
if (thread_type_a) {
    .....
}

__syncthreads();  // creates common barrier
```
This produces 0 errors.  The numerical tests passed and after benchmarking 100k cached + 1k prompt + 256 generated tokens produced almost no performance change.
Measured change:  improved prompt processing by 0.43% and token generation by 0.15%, so no measurable performance regression.

## Additional information
- https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/#thread-block-synchronization-functions
- https://docs.nvidia.com/compute-sanitizer/ComputeSanitizer/index.html#synccheck-tool

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: yes, GPT-5.6 Sol. I was doing performance optimizations for qwen 3.8 27B and it identified this issue during some FlashAttention work.

title: ggml : fix dimension and stride truncation in ggml_permute
body:
## Overview

Preserve tensor dimensions and byte strides in `ggml_permute` using `int64_t` and `size_t`, avoiding truncation through `int`.

## Additional information

`ggml_permute()` copies tensor dimensions (`int64_t`) and byte strides (`size_t`) through temporary `int` arrays. Values exceeding `INT32_MAX` are truncated before being assigned back to the output tensor.

For example, an F32 tensor shaped `[1536, 2048, 288, 1]` has:
```
      nb[3] = 1536 * 2048 * 288 * 4 = 3,623,878,656 bytes
```
This exceeds `INT32_MAX` (2,147,483,647). On the affected platform, conversion to `int` produces `-671088640`. Converting that negative value back to 64-bit `size_t` produces an enormous, invalid stride.

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES - AI assisted with diagnosis.

title: fix: correct overallocation when fitting speculative context without specified n_ctx
body:
## Overview

When running with `--fit-params` enabled and without specifying a `--ctx-size`, `load_model` overestimates the memory footprint of any draft/mtp context. It uses `n_ctx_train` to estimate speculative context size, rather than the actual context size. This is due to the fact that `n_ctx` is not determined until after the main model fit is run.

As a result, speculative contexts take up more VRAM than they should. On my 32 GB machine, I found that `--fit-params` was overestimating qwen3.6's MTP context by ~500 MiB.

Fixes #25408 

## Additional information

In this PR:
- a helper method now splits speculative context fit into two parts: a fixed component, and a per-ctx component
- the main model fit now uses the per-ctx overhead when calculating n_ctx
- n_ctx is now persisted after main model fit and used to init speculative context

title: context : do not re-reserve the scheduler on set_causal_attn
body:
The causal flag only changes the contents of the KQ mask inputs, not the graph topology, and llama_context::encode() already flips it without a reserve. llm_graph_params::allow_reuse() compares causal_attn, so the next decode still rebuilds the graph.

mtmd toggles the flag twice per image chunk. Each toggle forced a full sched_reserve (new scheduler + worst-case graph + compute buffers), which costs hundreds of milliseconds at high n_ctx. On video inputs that was two reserves per frame and made video processing crawl.

## Overview

Remove `sched_need_reserve = true` from `llama_context::set_causal_attn()` while preserving its early return and assignment.

Changing `cparams.causal_attn` affects only the values written to the KQ mask by `set_input_kq_mask`; it does not change graph topology or tensor sizes. The existing graph-reuse check includes `causal_attn`, so changing the flag still causes the next decode to rebuild the graph inside the already-reserved buffers.

This also makes `set_causal_attn()` consistent with `llama_context::encode()`, which temporarily changes `cparams.causal_attn` around `process_ubatch()` without requesting a scheduler reserve.

## Additional information

The issue is especially visible with mtmd because `tools/mtmd/mtmd-helper.cpp::scope_non_causal` disables causal attention before every image chunk and restores it afterward. Before this change, both calls triggered a full scheduler reserve.

At `n_ctx = 262144` with two slots, each reserve took approximately 700 ms. At `n_ctx = 131072`, each took approximately 330 ms and allocated a 612 MiB CUDA-host compute buffer. GPU utilization remained around 3% while one CPU core was saturated.

Benchmarks from a CUDA build on an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell using Gemma 4 31B Q4_K_M, two slots, `--kv-unified`, flash attention, and the same server flags before and after:

| Configuration    | Input                                       |  Before |                After |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------- | ------: | -------------------: |
| `n_ctx = 131072` | 10-second clip, 10 frames, 4,527 tokens     | 10.46 s |               3.18 s |
| `n_ctx = 131072` | Single-image embedding decode               |  405 ms |                66 ms |
| `n_ctx = 262144` | 10-second clip                              |  18.2 s |                3.3 s |
| `n_ctx = 262144` | 280-second clip, 280 frames, 114,949 tokens |   489 s | 118 s / 978 tokens/s |

After the change, verbose logs show only the four startup reserves. Output-generation performance was unchanged.

Output quality and causal-attention restoration were checked with:

* Video description
* Two images in one message with thinking enabled
* Tool calling
* A text-only follow-up after image input (`17 × 23 → 391`)

Not yet tested:

* Audio chunks, which use the same path
* M-RoPE vision models such as Qwen VL
* CPU-only backends
* `--no-mmproj-offload`

A possible follow-up is to decode consecutive image chunks in a single non-causal operation. Their encodings are already batched up to `--mtmd-batch-max-tokens`; batching their decode would also reduce per-frame decode overhead.

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: Yes: Claude Fable 5.1 was used to find this bug and to do benchmarking.

Nothing regresses: the lowest cell is 0.999×. The small gain is consistent and reproducible, but it does not come from the kernel — it comes from cheaper lookup.

`find_cfg` performs a linear table scan. For this workload, M4 Max often misses the exact bucket and falls back to the default config; the old path can scan the full table up to four times, including redundant retries through the family representative SKU (which is M4 Max itself for family 9).

Keying by family removes those redundant scans and searches a table **3.8× smaller**, reducing lookup cost from **2149 ns to 282 ns per call**. This also explains the small gains in cells where the selected config is unchanged.


None of this says the pooled rows pick faster kernels. In-sample they are 98.5% of per-device tuning at the attention level — marginally slower — which end to end is below what this test can resolve.

title: ggml-cpu: add repack GEMM and GEMV for floating-point
body:
## Summary
This PR adds repacking and GEMM/GEMV kernels for floating-point (FP16  and FP32) for RVV (with the `zvfh` extension).

## Key Changes
- Added RVV kernels for GEMM with tiling:
  - `7 x {16, 32, 64, 128}` (selected based on VLEN)
- Added RVV kernels for GEMV with tiling:
  - `1 x {16, 32, 64, 128}` (selected based on VLEN)
- Added scalar functions for repacking. They support arbitrary tile sizes.  
- Generic scalar fallbacks for GEMM/GEMV operations. 
- `ggml_quantize_mat_t` is refactored to `ggml_repack_mat_t` to allow for a common interface for both quantization and floating-point repacking.
- Additional template parameter `NB_ROWS` added to select the number of rows to interleave for repacking. Previously, this was fixed at `4`.

## Tile Sizes

The repack operation interleaves `N` rows of `activations` with an interleave size of `K`, and `M` columns of `weights` with an interleave size of `K`.

`NxK` is fixed at `7x1`. This introduces 7 accumulators with `LMUL=4` (7 x 4 = 28 registers), each accumulating `M` results.

`M` is varied based on the available VLEN:

| VLEN | Tile Size (N x M x K) |
| -------- | ----------- |
| 128 | 7 x 16 x 1 |
| 256 | 7 x 32 x 1 |
| 512 | 7 x 64 x 1 |
| 1024 | 7 x 128 x 1 |

`M` is the maximum number of values that can be loaded in (LMUL=2 for F16, LMUL=4 for F32).
  
## Testing
Kernels were functionally tested on QEMU for VLENs (128-bit, 256-bit, 512-bit and 1024-bit) for a range of input sizes.

## Benchmarking Results
End-to-end benchmarking on  `BananaPI-BPI F3 (VLEN=256)` with `llama-bench` (`Threads=8)`).

### Prefill / Prompt Processing (GEMM)

#### Tokens / Second

## Additional Notes
- Current fallback model requires every architecture to have a scalar fallback for each implementation. This creates a clutter in `arch-fallback.h` as `7xMx1` is very RVV-specific tiling, and should not be used by other architectures.
- `GEMM` reaches peak performance when the prompt is a multiple of 7 (for example, `prompt=28`). To handle leftovers, it defaults to `GEMV`, which impacts performance. Ideally, there should be leftover `Nx32` kernels which handle each leftover case from `2-6` leftover tokens. 

## Future Work
Subsequent PRs plan to add RVV kernels for quantization types, as well as extend existing quantization support to other VLENs.

## References
The selection of the tiling `7x32x1` is based off of the `mmt4d` kernel in IREE for RVV: https://github.com/iree-org/iree/pull/20263

title: llama : fix K/V and recurrent state cleanup after failed restores
body:
## Overview

A failed per-sequence state restore can remove sequence metadata while leaving K/V or recurrent-state tensor data written by the failed restore.

Buffer-backed restores can also leave deferred writes pending, allowing them to be applied after cleanup.

This PR contains failed restores by:

* clearing affected K/V or recurrent-state tensor data;
* discarding deferred writes after cleanup and before the reader is destroyed;
* applying the same deferred-write cleanup to whole-context buffer restores;
* validating restored `cell_count` values before they are used for allocation or target-range setup;
* cleaning up an already-restored attention state when a later recurrent-memory restore fails in `llama_memory_hybrid`.

Failures before modifying the target sequence leave it unchanged. After modification, the affected state is removed rather than attempting transactional rollback. For `llama_memory_hybrid`, if the attention component has already been restored and the recurrent component then fails, the restored attention state is also cleared.

Fixes #27068.

## Additional information

The original issue was observed in the K/V cache, but the same failure-cleanup behavior is needed for recurrent memory.

Tensor cleanup is only performed after a valid target range has been established, so failures during metadata parsing do not clear unrelated cells.

Per-sequence restore now also validates `cell_count` against the available cache or recurrent-memory capacity before using it.

For `llama_memory_hybrid`, restore is sequential across the attention and recurrent components. If the recurrent restore throws after the attention restore has succeeded, the attention state restored for that sequence is cleared before the exception is rethrown.

The cleanup runs only on restore failure and does not affect successful restore or normal decoding.

### Tests

Added failed-restore regression coverage to `test-save-load-state`. Test 9 exercises corrupted buffer and file restores and runs through the existing architecture coverage, including hybrid models.

The test verifies that a failed restore leaves the affected sequence empty and does not leave tensor data that changes the logits of another sequence.

Local validation:

* `ctest`: 62/62 passed.
* Sequential run across 127 generated models: Test 9 PASS 123 / SKIP 4 / FAIL 0. The four skipped models (`dream`, `llada`, `llada-moe`, and `rnd1`) do not have memory.

CUDA validation and server-level fault injection with K/V and hybrid recurrent memory were also performed on an earlier base.

### Non-goal

This does not provide transactional restore. If a failed restore has already modified the target sequence, its previous contents are not reconstructed.

Cross-component cleanup is handled for `llama_memory_hybrid`, where attention restore can precede a failing recurrent restore. Equivalent cleanup for the other composite memory implementations (`llama_kv_cache_iswa`, `llama_memory_hybrid_iswa`, `llama_kv_cache_dsa_iswa`, and `llama_kv_cache_msa`) is not addressed by this PR.

The separate ON_DEVICE pre-validation issue is tracked in #27439.

title: server: fail initialization on async compute errors (#27309)
body:
## Overview

Fixes #27309.

A compute failure during context initialization can happen asynchronously. In that case, the initial `llama_decode()` may succeed, with the error only appearing when the backend is synchronized. The server could then print `model loaded` and report itself as ready, while requests later fail with `Compute error.`

Probe once more after synchronization so the backend error is caught, and fail initialization when the target context cannot evaluate.

## Additional information

Tested on Metal with and without warmup.

- An oversized context that hits OOM now fails during initialization.
- Normal context loading and completion still work.
- No-memory embedding models still load and serve embeddings.

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)

title: Make the drafter probabilistic and the target verify by rejection sampling for simple draft and MTP
body:
## Overview Today the model-based drafters throw away most of what the draft model knows. They run the sampler, discard its result, and take the top candidate, and the target then accepts that token only when its own draw lands on the same one. At temperature 0 that is the best available, since the target also always takes its top token. Above 0, they differ - the target samples while the draft still offers its single safest guess - and acceptance falls away as temperature rises. This PR adds two things to make this better. - Make the target use rejection sampling instead of requiring an exact match. - Despite the above, if the draft still gives its top candidate only, it evaluates to min(1, p(x)/1), same as p(x). Hence to make q(x) land, we make the draft probabilistic as well. This time the effective probability that a candidate is chosen from draft is sum_x(q(x)*min(1, p(x)/q(x))). The output distribution is preserved exactly. Accepting with `min(1, p/q)` and drawing the remainder from `norm(max(0, p - q))` is the standard construction; the residual cancels the over-delivery on tokens where the draft is more generous than the target. This is same as the mechanism in Leviathan et al. This PR applies to draft_simple and MTP only. Eagle3 is yet to be evaluated and DFlash is experimentally seen not to benefit with these changes. The likely reason for this is structural. DFlash reads every position of its block out of a single forward pass with no re-decode between them, so the positions are predicted jointly rather than conditioned on one another. Substituting a sampled token at one position leaves the rest of the block continuing from a token that was never drafted. The gain at that position is cancelled by the positions after it, which no longer follow from what was drafted — unlike draft-simple and draft-mtp, where each token is re-decoded and the substitution carries forward. A flag --spec-draft-sampling is added, controlling how the draft is sampled. It takes greedy or probabilistic, defaulting to greedy. This matches vLLM's convention, where draft_sample_method takes the same two values and also defaults to greedy. I have run sweeps with -bs enabled and disabled along with the changes in this PR. Based on the logs obtained, this PR does not affect the functionality of backend sampling, which ensures that the target sampling chain already happens on the GPU. With -bs on, I see the same accepted length and 1-2% change in throughput, which is consistent with what is observed on the master branch with -bs enabled.
Performance

Two machines, eight model configurations each, 11 temperatures from 0.0 to 1.0. Every run is 12 prompts of 256 tokens at --spec-draft-n-max 3, the shipped default. Temperature 0.0 is the control. title: llama : preserve original batch order for speculative decoding layer inputs
body:
## Overview

When llama.cpp splits a batch to process multiple requests (concurrency > 1), it can change the token order. With separate KV streams, the hidden states could reach DFlash in that changed order even though it expected the original order. This meant the draft sometimes received another token's hidden states, reducing acceptance.

The fix remembers each token's original position and puts its hidden states back in the correct row before DFlash reads them. This fixes the mismatch while keeping separate KV streams.

## Results

Tested on SPEED-Bench using Qwen3.8-27B with its DFlash2 drafter, both quantized to Q4_K_M with concurrency = 16.

Mean acceptance length (AL) improved from **3.3531 to 3.9211**, a **16.94% increase** overall.

| Coding | 3.4884 | 4.0518 | +16.15% |
| Humanities | 3.2335 | 3.6909 | +14.14% |

title: openvino : report the device allocation limit to ggml
body:
## Overview

OpenVINO reported no GPU allocation limit to ggml, so a single buffer for the whole kvcache was always used. A GPU caps the size of a single memory object and a model could fail to load if the context was too large (e.g. on an iGPU with a 4 GiB cap). With the real limit ggml splits the buffer and large contexts work.

Fixes https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/29087. See that issue for more details including reproduction steps.

## Implementation details

The real limit is taken by getting the `CL_DEVICE_MAX_MEM_ALLOC_SIZE` property from a `clGetDeviceInfo` call once at GPU initialization phase. In case of failed query - old `unlimited` value is used as fallback, which is the same as previous behavior ensuring no regression.

## Verification

Checked that all models mentioned in the issue as failing with large enough contexts now pass on my iGPU (UHD Graphics 770)

| model | context enough to cause error (see the issue) | context checked | result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Llama-3.2-1B | 131071 | 131072 | pass |
| Llama-3.2-3B | 37449 | 65536 | pass |
| Qwen2.5-14B | 21845 | 22016 | pass |
| Qwen2.5-32B | 16383 | 16384 | pass |

The path on dGPU (Intel Arc Pro B70) has much larger limit (~30GiB). The code works as before in this path:  `alloc_tensor_range` uses one allocation because kvcaches are below larger limit.

Executing on CPU doesn't enter this code at all as before - unlimited value is used.

title: sycl : pinned memory uses right device context instead of 0
body:
## Overview

This is a fix for https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/28765.
Environment is a machine with 2 GPUs using different platforms. Running decode on a device with index 1 fails with false `UR_RESULT_ERROR_OUT_OF_DEVICE_MEMORY` on the path using `ggml_backend_sycl_get_tensor_async`. Root cause was `ggml_backend_sycl_host_malloc` always calling `get_device(0)`, not taking device index. At the upper layer the function caller `ggml_backend_sycl_device_get_host_buffer_type` ignored device number. See details in https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/28765

With this change there are multiple host `ggml_backend_buffer_type` instances instead of a singleton. Each instance is related to one device. Thanks to this a context related to output tensor device is selected during malloc and free.

Public parameterless function `ggml_backend_sycl_host_buffer_type` is left untouched with a comment that it pins memory on zero-index device, which may or may not cause problems if used with devices with other indices (this depends on devices' platforms). Decision to remove this function or not from public interface is out of scope of this bugfix PR.

## Verification

Tested on a machine with dGPU Arc B70 and iGPU UHD 770 on a clean upstream master and on the same master with the fix.

Without the fix: Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-Q4_K_M model fails when using index 1 GPU, passes on index 0 GPU. With the fix the model passes on both devices.

Tested iGPU being SYCL0 and dGPU being SYCL1. Tested also with iGPU being SYCL1 and dGPU being SYCL0 (by using `ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR` to permute devices).

## Additional information

Merging this PR...

1. will unblock work in https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/27689 
2. may (but also may not) fix https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/27888 whose conditions are very close to this one and observed behavior is the same

This issue revealed a problem in compute-runtime which returns `ZE_RESULT_ERROR_OUT_OF_DEVICE_MEMORY` instead of `ZE_RESULT_ERROR_INVALID_ARGUMENT`. That made people working on https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/27689 look for memory shortages and made their investigation work more difficult. I plan to fix this error code too.

title: server : do not forward --api-key-file to router-spawned child instances
body:
## Overview
In router mode, authentication belongs to the router. unset_reserved_args() already unset LLAMA_API_KEY, but did not unset LLAMA_ARG_API_KEY_FILE. When --api-key-file was passed, children re-validated against file keys only, causing clients using --api-key to 401 on chat completions (#28820). In addition, router internal calls without auth headers (such as POST /v1/streams/lookup and DELETE /v1/stream) were silently rejected with 401.

Unset LLAMA_ARG_API_KEY_FILE in unset_reserved_args() so no API keys reach child instances. This keeps keys out of child argv, ensures all keys the router accepts work end-to-end, and prevents router internal stream calls from 401ing.

Fixes #28820

## Additional information

Implements the approach suggested by @ServeurpersoCom in https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/28820#issuecomment-5662439730

title: sycl : support gated DSV4_HC_PRE and optional HC_POST comb matrix
body:
## Overview

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->
The SYCL backend implements two hyper-connection ops for DSV4-style models (`DSV4_HC_PRE` / `DSV4_HC_POST`). However, SYCL did not support the sigmoid gate nor the scale parameter, and would fall back to the CPU (unlike other backends like Metal and Cuda, which implement all parameters).
This PR enables gated / scaled HC to run in the SYCL context without fallback to the CPU, which aids graph recording / replay, but has little performance impact alone.
For `HC_POST`, we make the comb matrix optional (like on the CPU/CUDA  backend), which is how the qwen4exp model calls it, and this also prevents SYCL offloading.

As a small helper, I've moved the block sizes from magical number to a static constexpr for easier manipulation and tracking.

## Additional information

<!-- You can provide more details and link related discussions here. Delete this section if not applicable -->

title: fit : optimize for dense models
body: ## Overview For dense models, `--fit` moves whole layers to the CPU `-ngl` style, which is slow. This PR adds prioritization of what gets put on the CPU. The plateau is because the output tensor is large, so it leaves a lot of slack for context, at the same tensor placement. The drop at the end is where the regular `-ngl` kicks in and performance nears the original behaviour. ## Additional information This PR is a follow-up to my issue [#27987](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/27987), where doing the ordering automatically in `--fit` was suggested. Through testing I learned about other possible optimizations, so this PR includes a bit more than the issue proposed (like "output tensor" or "rest of layer" on the CPU, not just FFNs). ### `--fit` ordering Largest FFNs go first, then the rest of those layers (attention weights, norms, recurrent state) in the same order, then the output tensor, then the MTP layer, and then `-ngl` gets lowered only as a last resort, which causes the usual performance drop. #### Ordering cost Measured on Qwen3.8 27B UD3-Q4_K_M at 60k context as tg cost per MiB moved to the CPU (`-ot`, one at a time): | lever | µs/token per MiB | |---|---| | FFN tensors, K-quants | 12 | | FFN tensors, IQ3/Q3 (the smallest ones) | 16.5 | | rest of a layer, FFN already off | 13.5-15 | | output tensor, no MTP / MTP on | 12 / 13.5-23 | | MTP layer FFN | 15-20 | | `-ngl` (scales with context length) | 25-33 | - Sorting FFNs by size is close enough to sorting by cost. The smallest FFNs are the most expensive per MiB, so they end up last anyway. - FFNs before a layer's remainder: 4-9% faster than moving layer by layer. - The output tensor is large (1 GB on both model quants) and cheap without MTP, but the MTP draft runs it once per draft token, so it can get expensive, so I'm placing it after the layer remainders, but before MTP and `-ngl`. For tied embeddings (Gemma) it moves the GPU copy of `token_embd`. MoE fit ordering is unchanged. The fit takes up to about twice the test loads of master, ~1.5 s for me. ### Testing I have 1 GPU, so I added a guard against multiple GPU systems because I couldn't test that. Multiple GPU systems keep the previous `-ngl` behaviour. If someone tests this on multiple GPUs, the guard can be removed. Checked 18 GGUFs (Qwen 3.x dense/MoE, TinyLlama, phi 2, gemma 2-4, mamba, rwkv 6, OLMoE, falcon h1, LFM2, MiMo) via `llama-fit-params` to make sure the ordering holds. Loaded and filled Qwen 3.8 27B and Gemma 4 12B as seen in the charts. ### Not PR related issue that could affect performance `--fit` incorrectly calculates free VRAM. For me, the correct `--fit-target` values are between -400 and +200 (depending on the model and MTP use) to fully utilize my VRAM and not OOM crash upon use. Rough workaround: run the server, give it a big file to chew on, tell it to write a story, if it OOM crashes then raise `--fit-target`, if it doesn't then lower the value till it does, then raise it a step back. ## Requirements - I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md) - AI usage disclosure: YES, I used it to write the code, but I made the decisions and reviewed it.

title: common : end the URL authority at '?' so query-only URLs keep their query
body:
Fixes #28400

If a URL has a query string but no path, like `https://example.com?download=1`, `common_http_parse_url()` gets the host wrong. It only looked for the first `/` to find where the host ends. RFC 3986 says `?` ends it too, so that URL came out as `host=example.com?download=1` and `path=/`.

That broke two things. `common_http_client()` builds the `httplib::Client` from that host, so it tried to connect to a name that doesn't exist. And the query string never made it into the request.

The fix swaps the split to `rest.find_first_of("/?")`, so the host now stops at whichever of `/` or `?` comes first. Everything after that, including the leading `?`, is kept as the request path.

Hosts, ports, userinfo and bracketed IPv6 addresses parse the same as before. The only URLs that parse differently are the ones that used to end up with a `?` inside the host.

Since this parser is shared, the fix also applies to:
- `-mu` / `--model-url` downloads (`common/download.cpp`)
- `common/hf-cache.cpp`
- the CLI HTTP client
- the server CORS proxy

I added `tests/test-http.cpp` as a regression test. It checks the scheme, host, port and path for the query-only URL. It fails on `master` and passes with this change.

### Requirements

<!-- IMPORTANT: Please do NOT delete this section, otherwise your PR may be rejected -->

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: <!-- mention: YES / NO - if yes, describe how AI was used --> YES. I used AI to help write the regression test.

---

I ran both checks in an `ubuntu:24.04` Docker container.

**With the fix:** full CMake build of the test target with `-DLLAMA_FATAL_WARNINGS=ON`, then ran the test.

```

+ /build/bin/test-http
TEST-HTTP-EXIT=0
```



**What changed:**
